items.body: Add a viola, and the whole world changes. On Stella Maris, Pavia post-rockers Tristan de Cunha become a trio, thanks to Nicolò Vara, which moves their already orchestral sound to the realm of the majestic. Now in their tenth year, the band is still making waves, and these waves are larger than any that came before. The album is inspired by the followers of Our Lady Star of the Sea (as approved by the Catholic Church). One can see Mary on the cover, shrouded in mystery, the guiding star for those at sea. Through wind and storm, perils within and perils without, her prayers and those of her supplicants guide seafarers home. This is a great theme for a post-rock suite, allowing for peaks and valleys, high drama on the open seas, and grand spiritual themes. The album works best played as a single piece, unfolding as a suite. The opening notes are like a ship’s horn, cutting through the fog, stopping and restarting, underlining the tension. Vara enters swiftly like a tumultuous sea. The drummer adds a pulse. And then suddenly the ship pushes into gentler, ambient seas. Cymbals shimmer, the guitar refracts, the viola offers a meditation. And all this in the prelude alone! One barely notices as the piece tips into the title track, which bleeds reflection and even remorse in long, rolling tones: an early emotional highlight. To listen is to think of three sets of parties: the sailors, possibly lost at sea; the people left behind to wonder at wait; and the third, divine party, to whom both prior sets petition. The ominous “A Tidal Wave Shall Push Them to the Light” implies two kinds of light: safety and salvation, although death may lie between. The wave never breaks, but remains a constant shadow, ignoring nature’s laws, demanding divine intervention. After this, the album enters a zone of abstraction, like the dark imaginings of a fitful sleep, the sailors unaware of their fate, tortured by nightmares. The ship begins to steady in “Wound,” implying the wounds and thus the mercy of Christ: by his wounds we were healed. The spiritual associations are cemented in “The Veil” with the arrival of a subdued yet powerful choir. The Star of the Sea has intervened! This is the set’s high water mark, to which all builds and from which all subsides. When the strings enter, the song dives straight to the heart. In “Continuum,” the ship sets a course for home. For a decade, guitarist Francesco Vara and drummer Luca Scotti have been sailing the high seas alone. Nicolò Vara is a steadying force, echoing the bolstering presence of the divine. The hull is now stronger, the sails more flexible, the ship more confident in the storm. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Mind Maps 7 stands as another richly rewarding chapter in an extraordinary body of electronic music—one that continues to push gently at the boundaries of ambient, downtempo and sample-based composition without ever losing its sense of warmth or wonder. Long may these maps continue to unfold, pointing listeners towards the kind of electronic music that still feels capable of surprising, transporting and quietly reshaping the landscape around it. FSOL’s discography does not simply evolve; it mutates There are few artists in electronic music who have remained as resolutely unknowable as The Future Sound of London. They are the embodiment of an enigma. For more than thirty years Garry Cobain and Brian Dougans have operated as both pioneers and outliers, continually reshaping their own vocabulary through an ever-expanding catalogue of albums, EPs, archives and aliases. While countless contemporaries became defined by genres they helped create, FSOL have consistently resisted taxonomy, preferring intuition over orthodoxy and exploration over repetition. Their discography does not simply evolve; it mutates. Part of that mystery has always been embedded in their process. FSOL have rarely offered the listener an easy route map. Names, identities, boundaries and explanations are often blurred or deliberately withheld, allowing the music to exist first as an experience rather than as a product. In an age where everything is indexed, categorised and instantly explained, their continued commitment to ambiguity feels almost radical. The work arrives as a place to enter, not merely an object to consume. “In an age where everything is indexed, categorised and instantly explained, their continued commitment to ambiguity feels almost radical. The work arrives as a place to enter, not merely an object to consume.” ~Will Wonks History, however, tends to return to one moment. “Papua New Guinea” remains the unavoidable touchstone—not because it was their first great work, but because it captured electronic music standing on the threshold of possibility. Emerging from Britain’s bleep-and-clonk years, in parallel with Warp‘s formative identity and the rapid mutation of acid house, it proposed an altogether different future. Built from the haunting vocal of Dead Can Dance‘s “Dawn of the Iconoclast,” the cavernous bassline of Meat Beat Manifesto‘s “Radio Babylon” and additional textures from Circuit‘s “Shelter Me,” FSOL transformed familiar source material into something wholly original. Breakbeats displaced rigid four-to-the-floor momentum, ambient textures sat alongside uncompromising low-end pressure, while melody became both emotional and transportive. Toughness and tenderness occupied the same space without contradiction. Its influence is difficult to overstate. In much the same way that Talk Talk inadvertently sketched the blueprint for post-rock, “Papua New Guinea” suggested that dance music could become something beyond the dancefloor. It pointed towards the seed of what we now know as IDM, planting an idea that electronic music could be cerebral, emotional, fractured and exploratory without losing its physical connection to rhythm. From there, its influence would echo through jungle, intelligent techno, ambient, trip hop, breakbeat, chill-out, broken beat and countless hybrid forms that defined the decade. Whether directly or indirectly, it helped legitimize experimentation as a central impulse within electronic music rather than a curious diversion from it. A living organism, continually rewriting itself :: Alongside A Guy Called Gerald‘s “Voodoo Ray,” LFO‘s “LFO,” and Orbital‘s “Chime,” “Papua New Guinea” stands as one of those genuinely era-defining recordings that crystallized the cultural optimism of an impending post-Thatcher Britain. These were not merely club records. They reflected a generation discovering new communities, new aesthetics and new ways of imagining itself beyond the orthodoxies of the preceding decade. As ever, those radical impulses would eventually be absorbed into the machinery of mainstream culture, their once-disruptive edges softened through repetition and commodification. Yet the original spark remains unmistakable. To trace the genealogy of contemporary electronic music is, sooner or later, to arrive at The Future Sound of London. “Papua New Guinea” is more than a classic; it is an archetype, a permanent timestamp marking the moment electronic music realized just how expansive its vocabulary could become. “I’m attempting to describe something deeply that exists most completely as sculptured sound. Music, such as we have gifted here, at its most powerful, escapes the boundaries of moribund explanation.” ~Will Wonks As we move through the fourth decade since that breakthrough, Mind Maps 7 finds Cobain and Dougans turning their attention towards the work of others, continuing to reinterpret and reshape electronic music through the unmistakable FSOL lens. The archive is not a museum; it is a living organism, continually rewriting itself. Opening with clocolan, the collection sees FSOL reworking material by Jack Dangers as Meat Beat Manifesto, Humanoid—the long-running Brian Dougans alias—Pye Corner Audio, the inimitable cable.percussion, Plaid, Canopy of Stars, Ruxpin, Heogen, Sundial Aeon, Syl Kougaï, Christ., and Pentagrams Of Discordia. These are not conventional remixes so much as acts of transformation. Familiar structures are dismantled, atmospheres are reimagined and fragments are repositioned, while the essential character of each source remains just visible beneath the surface. Across familiar territories and unexpected detours, breaks cut and shuffle, atmospheres touch, fracture and transform. Acts of transformation :: The sublime reworking of Plaid‘s heartbeating “Reindeer” arrives as the standout for me, although that conclusion undoubtedly carries its own resonant bias as a lifelong fan of their magical oeuvre. Yet there is no noticeable drop in quality across the entire collection. Ultimately, there are limits to this same language when I’m attempting to describe something deeply that exists most completely as sculptured sound. Music, such as we have gifted here, at its most powerful, escapes the boundaries of moribund explanation. Perhaps that is why FSOL continue to endure as a trustworthy creative force while some of their contemporaries have found comfort in routine or the familiar pull of nostalgia. Their music has never sought definitive answers, only fresh routes through familiar terrain, treating every ending as the beginning of another possibility. Mind Maps 7 is another reminder that exploration, curiosity and reinvention remain fundamental to both the practice of being human and the act of making art. More importantly, it stands as another richly rewarding chapter in an extraordinary body of electronic music—one that continues to push gently at the boundaries of ambient, downtempo and sample-based composition without ever losing its sense of warmth or wonder. Long may these maps continue to unfold, pointing listeners towards the kind of electronic music that still feels capable of surprising, transporting and quietly reshaping the landscape around it. Artwork by Grid Pattern. Mind Maps 7 is available on Touched Music. [Discogs]The post V/A :: FSOLdigital Presents Mind Maps 7 (Touched Music) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Biogenes Resources is a testament to what a new generation of Russian electronic artists would do. The hope and whimsy that permeate the album hark back to a time of potential, where possibilities stretched across the many time zones of the vast Eastern land. In this reproduction, using the original MIDI files, the past reminds us of both the preciousness of our freedom of expression and that such expression can never be stifled. An expansive and playful brand of electronics Biogenes Resources by Novel 23   In some strange twist of history, the Soviet Union seems almost closer now than it did in 1997. Russia has returned a society where silence is the expectation. The hope, or the supposed hope, that came in 1991 has faded as a new form of repression has taken hold. Despite this, there were years of musical rejuvenation. Electronic music bloomed. Talent that had taken root now had the freedom to scatter their sounds. Labels like Art-Tek were seminal in this movement with homegrown artists offering brand new ideas and energy. Founded by Roman Belavkin, aka Solar X, and Yura Moorush, Art-Tek attracted a new generation of music machinists. Names like Ambidextrous, EU, Fizzarum and Novel 23 became part of the family as a smattering of CD and vinyl slowly became available. You’d have to have had your ear to the ground to have come across the releases, but the artists involved spread their wings to labels like City Centre Offices and Lo Recordings while also inspiring and appearing on contemporary imprints like SEALT. Russian musicians have found it difficult to distribute their music as they once did, current sanctions meaning that Bandcamp cannot be used to sell. The brief light of freedom has been consumed by shadow. Nevertheless, pinpricks of hope still shine through. Novel 23, Roman Belousov, has decided to return, to return to his very beginnings. In 1997 his debut album came out on Art-Tek, one of the label’s first releases. Biogenes Resources originally appeared as a cassette tape, Soviet analog machines employed to create an expansive and playful brand of electronics. Fast forward thirty years, Belousov has remade the entire album using the same equipment. Art-Tek founder, Solar X, recalls that “this was the first music Roman produced I remember, he began writing it in 1996 after we met, and I encouraged him to buy Soviet synths. One of the main instruments there was Electronica EM-25”. It is this very same machine that has been dusted off to recreate the eleven works of the collection. A narrative of nature runs through the album :: Novel 23’s first release, the album is filled with charm and the innocence of a young artist. For those not familiar with Belousov’s work, immediate comparisons would be the likes of Bochum Welt or CiM. Here, the mood is somewhat more subdued. Soft synth-lines swirl below acid globules and brittle beats in the opening “Dawn Without Hope.” An off-kilter melody bends and bulges in the fragile “Clear Sky” before the meandering brightness of “Not Caught Fish.” A narrative of nature runs through the album with track titles such as “Transparent Brook” and “Light Storm Cloud.” Each work holds the seed of the talent that Novel 23 would become. The absorbing and unsettling quality of “Cool Sun Rays”, the texture and warmth of “Thick Mist in Lowland” and understated elegance of “Sunset for Rain” resonate as a precursor to Belousov’s later audio explorations. “Change of Wind & Temperature” is the most immersive offering of the album. Brimming with enthusiasm, flashes of the later Novel 23 sound and style come to the fore. Biogenes Resources is a testament to what a new generation of Russian electronic artists would do. The hope and whimsy that permeate the album hark back to a time of potential, where possibilities stretched across the many time zones of the vast Eastern land. In this reproduction, using the original MIDI files, the past reminds us of both the preciousness of our freedom of expression and that such expression can never be stifled. Biogenes Resources is available on Art-Tek. [Bandcamp] Biogenes Resources by Novel 23The post Novel 23 :: Biogenes Resources (Art-Tek) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Human Music: Live Improvisations I serves as both a statement and a philosophy. What I hear is a collection of live performance recordings, each about 6-7 minutes long, one player/performer using layers and loop technology to play many instruments at once in a live setting, creating classical flavored music improvisations and instrumental expressions with haunting vocals that are entirely without word content, just emotional tones that bend and transmit. Emotional responses that define genuine human expression Human Music: Live Improvisations I by Jessica Roch   Jessica Roch brings her insightful studio mixing skills to these improvised multi-instrumental tours de force, drawn from performances captured between 2022 and 2025 in concert halls, intimate venues, and assembly rooms across England. Human Music: Live Improvisations I is a document of spontaneity, vulnerability, and presence that was written, recorded, produced, arranged, and mixed, as well as performed live by Jessica Roch on violin, synth, vocals, pianos, vibraphone, many pedals and (many) electronics. In this six track anthology the audiences are breathless, each piece unfolds in real time, free from predetermined outcomes, embracing the subtle imperfections, fleeting decisions, and emotional responses that define genuine human expression. She also created the cover art, an eye-catching expression of photographic compositing and imagery, with the album’s physical graphic design and layout by zakè. Human Music serves as both a statement and a philosophy. What I hear is a collection of live performance recordings, each about 6-7 minutes long, one player/performer using layers and loop technology to play many instruments at once in a live setting, creating classical flavored music improvisations and instrumental expressions with haunting vocals that are entirely without word content, just emotional tones that bend and transmit. Human Music, to me, describes how the focus is on truth and insight. There is risk taking, being honest and thorough, as well as staying nimble. These performances were each invented on the fly. These recordings are not polished constructions assembled from endless revisions, but living moments captured as they happened, shaped by the atmosphere of the room, the energy of the audience, and the artist’s instinct in the moment. There is never any AI present here. Living moments captured as they happened :: In an era increasingly shaped by automation and algorithmic creation, Human Music celebrates the irreplaceable qualities of live performance: intuition, risk, connection, and the profound beauty found in uncertainty. “London Live Session, Oct. ’25” opens with a piano, which communicates empathy and intuition, never any urgency, just easy relaxing floating on the infinite sea, eased by repeating ethereal voices that haunt like a night-drawn candle would. At “Threadsafe, King’s Cross, Dec. ’24” there are flutes flying about all over the place, flickering and fluttering, followed by a robust violin session. We float around nicely for part of eternity while the heavenly vocal choir echoes somewhere above, and soon the cathedral is filled with so many voices, legions coming back together as one. The program at “St. John on Bethnal Green, Oct. ’24” starts with vocals and that big cathedral sound, in time a choir builds and soon the hot violin arrives and weaves around the choir refrains. The feeling is satisfying and peaceful, with a feeling of intimate intricacy. “A masterpiece of depth and warmth, wrapped in strange beauty surely evoked by classical wandering spirits.” ~Robin B. James “Liquid Light Session One, Oct. ’22” starts off when the pianos interact, a violin is plucked delicately and very subtly, within and without. The vibraphone grooves in, sly and lean, forming a nice multilayered atmosphere of instruments and vocal presence. Later, at “Liquid Light Session Two, Oct. ’22” it feels like water is reflecting multicolored light, flickering and exploding as shadows silently signal a response. The violin somehow changes the feeling, and ghosts are musically gesturing in the background. For the final track, “Howard Assembly Room, Leeds, Jun. ’24” we start from plucked violin strings, layering behind a bright bowed story teller, leading into some fancy violin playing. This comes after as well as during the vocal moments, adding many serious details. Some are a little dark, perhaps slightly sad. Of course there are no words, the voices that join in next have a teasing warble, and the rare elvish fairies nearly yodel. Soon the violin becomes the main thing, finishing with a warm synth-orchestra memory invoking assemblage. Water is reflecting multicolored light, flickering and exploding :: Jessica Roch is a London based, award winning composer, multi instrumentalist, sound designer, and improviser. In 2025, she received a Composer Spotlight Award at the Production Music Awards. She has recently performed at Cafe OTO and is a co-founder and director of The London Ambient Orchestra. Her solo work moves fluidly across genres, weaving ambient and electronic textures with elements of minimalism, jazz, folk, and experimental music. A classically trained violinist and pianist, Jessica creates music for film, games, and contemporary media, while also collaborating as a session musician with artists including Super Furry Animals. Jessica‘s composition Pandemonium: Music for Parakeets, was created as part of a cross disciplinary artistic collaboration, and was featured at The Design Museum as part of the Artificial exhibition, where it was on display throughout the summer season. Recently speaking about her debut album on Past Inside the Present, Jessica clarifies her intention. “This album is an unambiguous protest and rejection of AI-generated “music.” Human Music: Live Improvisations I, is imperfect, it is raw and it is unpredictable. That is the beauty of live improvisation. It is innately human.” “This album is an unambiguous protest and rejection of AI-generated “music.” Human Music: Live Improvisations I, is imperfect, it is raw and it is unpredictable. That is the beauty of live improvisation. It is innately human.” ~Jessica Roch Beautifully curated from an extensive collection of live performances, the album was mixed by Jessica herself and mastered with remarkable sensitivity by James Bernard at Ambient Mountain House. Together they preserve the immediacy and emotional depth of each performance while allowing every nuance, resonance, and breath of the room to remain intact. The result is a deeply personal body of work that stands as both an artistic statement and a testament to the enduring power of human creativity. Human Music: Live Improvisations I was shrinkwrapped, pressed, manufactured, and assembled in Ontario, Canada, with an edition of 200, glass-mastered, silkscreen printed CDs housed in a 4-panel, 300g satin cardstock Digipak with a clear cd tray. Human Music: Live Improvisations I is a masterpiece of depth and warmth, wrapped in strange beauty surely evoked by classical wandering spirits. Human Music: Live Improvisations I is available on Past Inside the Present. [Bandcamp] Human Music: Live Improvisations I by Jessica Roch  The post Jessica Roch :: Human Music: Live Improvisations I (Past Inside the Present) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Prince Alla has been singing roots since the 1970s, and on “Jah Is My Rock” his voice sits over a riddim that came together on the Spanish coast. Born Keith Blake in Kingston in 1950, he made his name with Bertram Brown‘s Freedom Sounds label, cutting “Stone” over a King Tubby dub mix and following it with “Bucket Bottom“. That same open-throated, declamatory delivery runs through this one too, and the title leans on the old Psalm line about God as a rock. The riddim is the work of Hal C, the Alicante producer Mario Coloma, who came up through the Barcelona reggae scene and now runs Piramid Records. He laid the track down at his own studio, then brought in players from across the map to finish it. Karl Wright cut the drums in the United States, Roberto Sánchez handled the backing vocals at his A-Lone Ark Muzik Studio in Santander, and Danny Trees mixed and mastered. It lands as the label’s fourth 7″, a black-vinyl 45 in a full-colour sleeve, with a dub of the rhythm on the flip. Stream and get your copy of “Jah Is My Rock” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Prince Alla – Jah Is My Rock (Remix by Hal C) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — There is a particular kind of return that has nothing to do with nostalgia and everything to do with stubbornness.Opus Avantra were born in the Veneto in the early seventies out of an idea rather than a line-up: AVANguardia and TRAdizione, avant-garde and tradition, welded into a single word by the soprano Donella Del Monaco, the pianist and composer Alfredo Tisocco, the philosopher Giorgio Bisotto and the producer Renato Marengo. Their 1974 debut, universally known as Introspezione, remains one of the strangest objects in the entire Italian catalogue of that decade, a record that belongs to progressive rock mostly because nobody could think where else to file it, and which earned the group a place on the Nurse With Wound list among the true outsiders of European music.Lord Cromwell Plays Suite For Seven Vices followed in 1975, then long silences broken by Strata in 1989, Lyrics in 1995, and Venetia et Anima in 2003. Sixteen years later, on the fourteenth of January 2019, Rosa Rosae appeared, produced once again by Renato Marengo, the same man who had produced the debut forty five years earlier, under the artistic direction of Tisocco. Whatever else it is, it is a circle closing.The record is credited to Donella Del Monaco, Paolo Troncon and the Opus Avantra Ensemble, and that order of names is accurate. Del Monaco writes all the texts and sings them, moving between Latin, Italian and French with a delivery that comes from the conservatory and from a family where the surname Del Monaco meant something before she ever recorded a note. Troncon composes, arranges and directs, and his training is classical and contemporary rather than rock: he writes in polyrhythmic and contrapuntal forms rather than in verses and choruses, which is precisely why this is not a pop record wearing a costume.The ensemble is Mauro Martello on flutes, saxophones and duduk, Laura Balbinot on cello, Andrea De Nardi on keyboards and Giorgio Cedolin on drums, expanded by accordions, a second cello, tenor saxophones and percussion. The guest list reads like a summit of the Italian seventies: Tony Esposito, who had already played on the 1974 debut, Lino Vairetti of Osanna, Jenny Sorrenti of Saint Just, and Alberto Radius of Formula 3, whose contribution here now carries an unintended weight, since he died in February 2023.The theme is the rose and therefore love, declined between sacred and profane, devotion and desire, with the two poles deliberately confused and sometimes inverted. It is a concept album in the old and serious sense of the term, not a suite with a title stuck on afterwards.A word on sequencing, because it matters. The 2019 CD ran nine pieces and opened with the accordion led lyricism of Nuvole Bianche. The later vinyl edition carries eleven, fully resequenced, adding the previously unreleased L'Angelo Caduto, restoring Aurea Lyra in its original version rather than the CD reworking, and bringing Sceleratus back as a closing reprise. That order opens with the darkest music on the record and holds the warmth in reserve, which strikes me as the truer shape of the work.The track-by-track below follows the vinyl sequence.- Sceleratus: the severest thing here, sung in Latin, with Lino Vairetti's powerful Mediterranean baritone answering Del Monaco line for line. Exorcism and mysticism circling each other. As an opening statement it warns you immediately that this will not be comfortable listening.- Mandala: an instrumental in all but atmosphere, built on the interlocking percussion of Tony Esposito and Gabriele Bruzzolo over Troncon's piano, with Andrea Martin's tenor saxophone tracing long lines above. The most openly rhythmic piece on the album, and the clearest link back to the debut.- Aurea Lyra (original version): piano by Dimitri Romano, accordion, cello and percussion, a chamber ensemble rather than a band. The original reading is drier and less upholstered than the one issued on CD, and it gains from that.- Pi Greco: the shortest and most abstract passage, a piece of pure construction whose title tells you everything about the intention. It functions as a hinge rather than a destination.- Rosa Rosae: the title track, and the centre of gravity. Tenor saxophone, accordion, cello and piano weave around Del Monaco's voice in what is closest here to a genuine song, though the counterpoint never relaxes into accompaniment. The rose as flower and as rosary, both at once.- L'Angelo Caduto: the previously unreleased piece, and no mere appendix. The fallen angel is the natural counterpart to the diabolic material of Sceleratus, and it sits squarely inside the concerns of the record rather than beside them. Its absence from the CD now feels like an omission.- Nuvole Bianche: the accordion of Mirko Satto and Troncon's piano, the most immediately beautiful thing on the album and the piece that once opened it. Placed here, deep into the second side, it arrives as relief rather than as invitation, which suits it better.- Cyrcles: Alberto Radius plugs in and plays, unmistakably, with that liquid seventies tone set against Tommaso Troncon's tenor saxophone. A deliberate homage to the decade the group came from, and now an elegy as well.- Vento Del Nord: written by Del Monaco with Mauro Martello, and the one duet on the record, with Jenny Sorrenti. Two voices that could easily have fought each other and instead lean together. Quietly the most moving few minutes here.- Ineffabile Realt�: Troncon alone at the piano. After everything that has preceded it, the austerity feels earned rather than imposed.- Sceleratus (Reprise): the Latin returns, briefly, and the door closes on the same shadow it opened with.Rosa Rosae asks something of the listener, and it does not pretend otherwise. Those who come to Opus Avantra hoping for the corrosive weirdness of Introspezione will find this more measured, more written, more willing to be beautiful; the fracture lines of 1974 have been smoothed by fifty years of thinking about the same problem. There are moments where the chamber writing verges on the decorous, and the abstract interludes will lose the impatient.Yet the ambition is intact and entirely unfashionable: a group that has spent half a century refusing to choose between the conservatory and the rock stage, still refusing, still finding new ways to hold the two apart without letting either win. Del Monaco's voice has darkened and gained gravity, Troncon's writing gives it architecture worthy of it, and the guests are used as colours rather than as selling points.This is a late chapter, and it knows it, but it is a rich one and it belongs on the shelf beside the records that made the name. An excellent album from a band that never learned how to be ordinary.My rating: 4/5.Bassano del Grappa (Italy), August 2026

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 980Porcupine Tree is an English progressive rock band that was formed in 1987 in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire. The band consists of a mix of prog rock, psych rock, avant-garde experimentalism and heavy metal. Despite this, Wilson doesn't have the same opinion. He mentions that Porcupine Tree's music is very simple, without complex elements. The complexity is in the production, in the way the albums are constructed. His first recordings "On The Sunday Of Life..." released in 1992 and "Up The Downstair" released in 1993, contain Wilson's first compositions, reminiscent of the cosmic rock of old glories like Pink Floyd and Eloy, but also resemble of the ambient rock from some contemporary bands like Ozric Tentacles. Wilson played all the instruments and did the drum programming. In addition, he invited some guest musicians to complete the picture on those works. By recording his acclaimed third album "The Sky Moves Sideways" released in 1995, which is the subject of this review, Wilson makes Porcupine Tree a true band. The new group received acclaim from critics around the world who describe the band as "The Pink Floyd of the new century".So, "The Sky Moves Sideways" is the third studio album of Porcupine Tree that was released in 1995. The line up on "The Sky Moves Sideways" is Steven Wilson (vocals, electric and acoustic guitars, bass guitar, keyboards, flute, tapes and programming), Richard Barbieri (keyboards and electronics), Colin Edwin (bass and double bass guitars) and Chris Maitland (drums and percussion). "The Sky Moves Sideways" had also the participation of Suzanne Barbieri (vocals), Theo Travis (flute), Gavin Harrison (drums overdubs) and Rick Edwards (percussion), all as guest musicians.After some success achieved with their previous albums, Wilson decided it was time for the band to hit the road, but for that he would have to have full-time musicians around. So he recruited the talented Richard Barbieri, Colin Edwin and Chris Maitland. Originally, the album should have been released as a single track, an epic work of about 50-minutes. However, this version was never finished, but divided into two parts which added up to about 36-minutes that begin and end the album, following an idea similar to that of Pink Floyd in "Wish You Were Here", with "Shine On You Crazy Diamond". In general, "The Sky Moves Sideways" walks in the footsteps of Pink Floyd, like no other work of the band, with a modern approach. With this work, the band manages to create a great album that picks up the tempo at the right places with rocky excursions where no boredom is and there's always something to discover even after many runs.The original version of "The Sky Moves Sideways" has six tracks. As I mentioned above, the title track suite is divided in two parts, opening and closing the original album. At its core, it was constructed and recorded alone by Wilson, but had overdubs by each of the three new members of the band, although Maitland didn't replace the drum machine, but only played the congas. The shortest recordings filling the middle of the album remained completely recorded solo. The piece is made in the best space rock style with the atmospheric sounds of Pink Floyd. The main passages are based on improvisations. Even so, the moods and sections are always well structured, making the music develop in an involving and dynamic way. As the suite winds toward its conclusion, some of the earlier instrumental themes are reprised. This suite is a masterpiece. "Dislocated Day" with its Oriental mood and melody is an excellent and very dark song, with a strong and emotive guitar riff that glides through the song in a very solid way. Solid are also the other instruments that energize the music with the maximum force. "The Moon Touches Your Shoulder" is a kind of an introspective ballad. It features beautiful acoustic guitar chords surrounded by lush keyboards and Wilson's airy vocals. The second half of the track is when things get more intense. Layers of sound introduce a kind of a guitar cacophony that settles down and carries us to the next track. "Prepare Yourself" is a very short instrumental featuring a good guitar work over an atmospheric keyboard and subtle bass drum beats. "Moonloop" seems to have been released in countless versions and lengths. It was created on completely different principles than the rest of the album. In the absence of Barbieri, and with the percussionist Edwards, the band entered the studio to record an improvisation eventually completing the repertoire of the album. It comes a bit close to the sound of the central piece with its expansive space rock passages.Conclusion: "The Sky Moves Sideways" is one of the albums to indicate to someone who doesn't know the band's work yet. On it, they actually performed as a band for the first time. The album represents a turning point in the band's work. Overall, "The Sky Moves Sideways" is an excellent example of the new psychedelic music style. This is probably, for me, the most atmospheric Porcupine Tree's album. "The Sky Moves Sideways" has a lot of moody, hypnotic and deep musical atmospheres. This is really an entertaining journey of discovery through Wilson's cosmos of sound. "The Sky Moves Sideways" is undoubtedly a masterpiece where each song is well arranged, well performed and well written.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

The last three studio albums are very good and they are each very unique. Three Sides of One is reflective on growing older, technology and the spiritual world. Excellent work.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — The third studio album from Norwegian band Seven Impale is definitely one of the long-awaitedprogressive rock releases of the decade, as it arrives seven years after their previous work'Contrapasso'. Seven Impale is a six-piece band that plays a pretty complex and theatrical style ofprogressive rock - their sound is heavily informed by the avant-garde rock scene as much as it is byclassic prog acts like Crimson and Van der Graaf. One could say their music is wilder than �nglag�rdand Ankedoten, yet it is no less sophisticated than the output of bands like Shamblemaths or Birdsand Buildings. Ideally, Seven Impale play a fusion-inspired modern rendition of retro prog; one thatis playful and dense, but also compositionally astute. And this is precisely what I admire abouttheir third album 'Summit' - a relentless record made up of four epics replete with tremendousmusical ideas, downright anxious instrumental sections, an interesting predisposition to dissonance,and an infectious energy.The titles of the four tracks suggest a mythological thread that underpins the concept of thisrecord. The epic nature of the music is then certainly befitting for such a conceptual thread, asthe four large pieces of heavy avant-prog deliver an in-your-face technicality mixed up with theband's pleasantly theatrical delivery. Lots of saxes and analog synths appear on this album, whichhas righteously reminded some listeners of Wobbler. But unlike their compatriots, Seven Impaleincorporate gnarly guitar riffs into their music, bringing in an almost sludgy feel to the heaviertracks. And this album certainly does not shy away from displaying pounding sections of heavy prog.All four compositions on 'Summit' are around the ten-minute mark, and their usual structure involvesan instrumental intro, followed by a swift transition into the main verse (and this is where themore intense or unusual ideas enter), leading up to a chorus that could be anything from cerebraland anthemic to crazy and surreal, after which an extended instrumental section brings thatexplosion of hectic ideas, complex interplay between the different instruments, and an overalleccentric feel. I cannot decide if I like 'Hunter' or 'Hydra' more, but the 13-minute album closer'Sisyphus' is up there with the best material on 'Summit', which to me is nothing short of astunning album. Highly recommended contemporary jazz-prog.

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — Forty six years passed between the celebrated 1972 debut of Reale Accademia di Musica and this second album, one of the longest gaps between two releases in the history of Italian rock.Guitarist Pericle Sponzilli, the sole returning member from the original lineup, reactivated the name in 2018 after being invited in September 2014 by organizer Guido Bellachioma to perform at the Progressivamente Free Festival alongside old companions from Fholks and acquaintances such as l'Uovo di Colombo, la Raccomandata con Ricevuta di Ritorno and Saint Just.Sponzilli took the decision partly because, in the intervening decades, other formations had used the historic Reale Accademia di Musica name for records that, in his view, did not represent the group's real legacy; Angeli Mutanti was conceived as what he considered the true second album of the band.Around him he assembled Fabio Liberatori, formerly of Stadio and a longtime collaborator of Lucio Dalla, on piano and keyboards, Erika Savastani, from Deserto Rosso, on vocals, Fabio Fraschini on bass, and Andy Bartolucci on drums, with guest guitarists Gianfranco Coletta, Nicola Di Staso and Fernando Fera contributing to individual tracks.Produced by Sponzilli and Liberatori themselves and released on the twenty eighth of February 2018 through M.P. & Records, in CD and in a limited edition of 300 white vinyl copies, the album carries artwork by Daniele Massimi built around a cover painting by Luciano Regoli, singer of La Raccomandata con Ricevuta di Ritorno, deliberately reviving the band's original 1972 logo while signalling a more contemporary sound.That contemporary sound is the record's defining choice. Angeli Mutanti bears almost no resemblance to the pastoral, mellotron soaked symphonic rock of the 1972 original. It favors instead compact, melody driven songwriting, warm ballads and soft rock textures, carried by the constant interplay between Sponzilli's raspy, characterful voice and Savastani's soulful, soaring one.Progressive elements surface less as extended instrumental workouts than as harmonic and structural details tucked inside otherwise accessible songs: unusual time signatures, brief but unmistakable echoes of Genesis, and orchestral flourishes that recall the golden age of Italian symphonic rock without ever trying to replicate it outright.The opening title track, Angeli Mutanti (Mutant angels), conjures in music and words a set of strange, nameless creatures that fly without wings or feathers, emotionally charged yet harmless, invisible demons without any plan. Musically it is a deceptively simple pop rock tune, lifted by light Hammond organ touches and unhurried, tasty guitar soloing.Alba (Dawn) follows in 5/4 time, its Genesis influenced writing plain to hear. The lyrics describe a metaphorical search for the rising sun and for a better day beyond time and space, a way out of a dark landscape built on lies, set against a bluesy tension and cold, Neo Prog style synthesizers.Johnny e Adele, a melancholic ballad featuring guest guitarist Gianfranco Coletta, paints a beautiful girl dancing on the beach to the notes of a guitar, and the dreams of the guitarist who loves her, colored throughout by warm Moog textures.Cosa nascondono le nuvole (What the clouds hide), with Nicola Di Staso guesting on guitar, opens with a knowing, cryptic echo of Genesis' Hairless Heart before settling into a dreamy, sleek pop rock groove that closes on a Mellotron laced outro clearly indebted to PFM, its words reaching toward far horizons.The Beat Goes On (come la canzone), featuring Fernando Fera on electric guitar, is the album's most straightforward moment, an elegant ballad built on soft, chiming guitar lines.Tempo (Time) turns toward more overtly progressive territory within the record's song based frame, its title alone signalling the preoccupation with time, memory and change that runs beneath even the album's most accessible melodies.A dritta San Salvador keeps the same balance of refined songwriting and understated instrumental interplay that defines the album's midsection, and has been singled out by Italian critics, alongside Io sono qui, Johnny e Adele, Cosa nascondono le nuvole and Tempo, for the sophistication of its trame, its narrative and musical weave.Una sola immagine (A single image), included only on the CD edition, stands apart for its authorship: the lyrics were written not by Sponzilli but by Nada Malanima, the celebrated Italian singer songwriter, lending the song a distinct voice within the album's otherwise unified lyrical perspective.Io sono qui (I am here), introduced by an almost solemn marching rhythm, is full of positive energy and describes an experience of daily rebirth guided by a sensei, a spiritual master whose words function like a chant to be followed in the morning light.The closing instrumental, La pista e il miraggio (The track and the mirage), mixes vintage sounds with exotic, almost cinematic atmospheres, arriving at symphonic passages that sit somewhere between PFM and Pink Floyd, and sending the album out on its most overtly progressive note.Angeli Mutanti was warmly received both in Italy and abroad, in Latin America, Japan, Korea, Canada and the Netherlands, and convinced even critics who had followed the historic Reale Accademia di Musica since the seventies, though a handful of more nostalgic voices wished for longer, more overtly progressive arrangements. Heard today, that same compactness feels less like a limitation and more like a deliberate choice.My judgment: 4 out of 5.Angeli Mutanti succeeds precisely because it does not try to be a sequel to the 1972 album in anything but name and spirit. It is instead a confident, contemporary record built on strong songwriting, a well balanced male and female vocal partnership, and just enough progressive character, in its harmonies, its guest guitar work, its unexpected time signatures, to remind the listener exactly which tradition it comes from.For anyone building a collection around the Italian progressive rock scene and its long, often improbable afterlives, this is a genuinely excellent addition, and a fitting first chapter to the story that Sponzilli would go on to continue four years later with Lame di Luce.

items.body: Review by Molloy — The new album by Compassionizer, "The Fellowship of the Mystery", continues Ivan Rozmainsky and histeam's bold experiments in musical artistry. As with the band's previous works, biblical referencesin the track titles provide the the album with structural cohesion and profound meaning. The albumopens with the evocative piece �To Abound and To Suffer Need", an emotional journey through shiftingmoods that oscillate between hope and despair, only to return triumphantly to hope. This powerfulinterplay of feelings sets the tone for the entire album. The second track, "Avenge Not Yourselves",immerses listeners in an atmosphere of austere contemplation. Its slow, meditative melodies inviteintrospection, preparing the audience for the album's subsequent explorations. This meditationseamlessly transitions into "To Direct Your Hearts into Love", a piece characterized by itssoothing, tranquil tones. As one of the album's standout gems, it radiates warmth and evokes a senseof gentle elevation. Among the most memorable tracks is "I Feel Shine of the Day", inspired by apoem by Ekaterina Vorotnikova. This bright and enchanting composition conjures an almost fairy-tale-like atmosphere, reminiscent of a dialogue between mythical beings?perhaps a fairy and a unicorn. Itbeckons listeners to embark on a magical adventure of life, celebrating the beauty and wonder ofexistence. Building on the theme of benevolent and mystical beings, the album explores the conceptof unseen helpers and miraculous saviors. The track "For Them Who Shall be Heirs of Salvation"reflects on the idea of angelic intervention. Its title alludes to the divine mission of beings sentto aid the heirs of salvation. The philosophical centerpiece of the album, "For the InvisibleThings", prompts reflection on the fleeting nature of the visible and the enduring significance ofthe unseen. Through its intricate melodies, the piece suggests that by reaching toward theinvisible, we may touch something eternal and profound. Finally, the titular track, "The Fellowshipof the Mystery", concludes the album triumphantly. It serves as a reflection on the journey ofenlightened souls, celebrating the mystery of existence and the divine threads that connect us all.With its harmonious blend of biblical themes, poetic inspiration, and musical ingenuity, "TheFellowship of the Mystery" takes listeners on a transcendent journey. It invites them to ponder thevisible and the invisible, the fleeting and the eternal, leaving an indelible impression of beautyand depth.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Sylvanite' is a 2003 studio album from Nad Sylvan, a singer and multi-instrumentalist who rose toprominence as the vocalist of Steve Hackett's Genesis Revisited touring band. Sylvan is also knownfor his collaborative work with members of The Flower Kings and Karmakanic as well as for being partof Inside Out Music's artists roster. And while most people recognize him for his recent prog rocksolo albums, very few are actually familiar with his earlier output, which is where we find thefunky pop-rock effort titled 'Sylvanite'. This is a commercially appealing album that exhibits astrong influence from pop artists like Prince and Blondie, and while it is enjoyable because it isaccessible, it is nowhere near the quality and sophistication of Nad Sylvan's prog rock efforts. Bythe way, he plays all the instruments here and is only joined by two female backing vocalists, whichis impressive. Songs that are worth checking out on this release are 'McNamara's Son', 'The GreatestStory Ever Told', 'Yellow Sky', and 'Bitch on Guitar'. Keep in mind that some tracks have a discovibe but play 'Sylvanite' if you want to hear some funky pop-rock and especially if you enjoy NadSylvan's vocals.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 2026 is the year of surprise-releases, and Boards of Canada definitely surprised their fanbase withthe release of a fifth studio album titled 'Inferno' on May 29, some thirteen years after'Tomorrow's Harvest'. The electronic duo consisting of Mike Sandison and Marcus Eoin has relied oncryptic messaging and atmospheric soundscapes ever since the 1998 release of their game-changing IDMcollection 'Music Has the Right to Children', and while this kind of music has never had a universalappeal in the mainstream, it has an undeniable edge that attracts listeners from variousbackgrounds. Going back to 'Inferno', this album echoes beautifully the darker and nostalgic tonesof earlier BoC albums. Perhaps a reaction to everything surrounding us nowadays, this eighteen-trackcollection expands the sonic palette of the Scottish duo and impresses with impeccable productionand a myriad of contemporary sounds. At its core a bleak-sounding album, however, this cinematic andexpansive release offers several intriguing electronic pieces, while it preserves the enigmaticnature of the duo's classic compositions.And still, no matter how many times I play 'Inferno', one unfavorable aspect of it always resurfaces- the styles and influences covered here can and do feel somewhat scattered. Of course, themasterful embodying of various sounds tends to compensate for the intimidating abundance ofdifferent genres of electronic music featured here, but this is something that underwhelmed mypersonal listening experience. Of the eighteen tracks on 'Inferno', I tend to really enjoy abouthalf of them, mildly appreciate roughly a quarter, and easily skip the rest. For example, 'Prophecyat 1420 MHz' enters with a moving eastern-inspired intro, which is followed by a haunting palette ofsounds that almost has a noir aesthetic to it. This darker aesthetic is then expanded on 'HydrogenHelium Lithium Leviathan', where the synths seemingly feed off each other, and on 'Somewhere RightNow in the Future', which reminds me of a gloomy daydream. 'Blood in the Labyrinth' is another trackexploring this somber atmosphere, and for whatever reason it reminds me of The Cure. At the sametime, the most intriguing pieces on 'Inferno' are the more ominous, occult-ridden tracks like'Father and Son' with its claustrophobic sound design, 'Naraka' and its wonderful tribal vibes, andthe uneasy but meditative piece 'The Word Becomes Flesh'.There are also many ambient-inspired instrumentals as well, and while some of them are lush andspacey, others feel like interludes or simply random entries. 'All Reason Departs' and 'MemoryDeath' are among the fine ones, while tracks like 'Arena Americanada', 'Into the Magic Land', and'You Retreat in Time and Space' strike me as forgettable. Overall, 'Inferno' is an excellentsurprise from Boards of Canada, and an album worthy of praise that offers a mostly alternativerendition of contemporary electronic music.

items.body: Review by kev rowland — I have not previously come across Arnaud Quevedo, but he is a French musician who has been teaching music at the Conservatoire since 2007 and has been performing under his own name since 2020. This live release from Arnaud Quevedo & Friends finds them performing in summer 2025 and features Quevedo (guitar, vocals, keyboards, alto sax) being joined by Noe Russeil (bass, vocals), Hortense Mailhos (drums), Julien Gomila (soprano & baritone saxophones) and Elo�se Baleynaud (lead vocals, keyboards).This is fusion which also contains some Crimson elements, and the band are very tight indeed, and can also be quite heavy at times, which makes for an interesting mix of styles and dynamics. The sax is an integral music as opposed to an afterthought, while the rhythm section certainly set the stage (the bass on this is stunning throughout) and Quevedo is a super guitarist. But, and it was fairly obvious there was a "but" coming, I am not a huge fan of Elo�se Baleynaud. We get quite a lot of scat, and much of her vocals are very much in the jazz vein, yet there are just too many times when she is not quite on point, which is fine when at a concert as people tend to overlook that but when listening to the performance it very much stands out, and in many ways lets down the rest. Her vocals have also been placed slightly to the rear in the mix, so she does not stand out as much as one would expect, and when she is providing backing vocals she seems more confident and at ease.The album is very loose, but also plenty tight, and I know if I was able to see them in concert I would, but whether I will return often to this CD is another matter altogether.

items.body: I’M NOT SURE IF THIS WORLD SURVIVES I CAN’T TELL YOU WHAT’S TRUTH OR LIES IT DOESN’T MATTER IF YOU’RE LEFT OR RIGHT WE’RE ALL DEAD UNLESS WE ALL UNITE After more than four decades spent turning political disgust, technological dread, and distorted guitars into blunt-force industrial rock, Ministry is preparing to shut down the machinery. Al Jourgensen has announced that the band’s forthcoming album, Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery), will be its last, bringing one of heavy music’s loudest and most unruly careers to a close on October 30 through Cleopatra Records. The first preview comes with Burned Out, a new single accompanied by a video directed by Joshua Bradford, formerly of Revolting Cocks. The title sounds like both a diagnosis and a resignation letter, which feels appropriate for a band that has spent decades staring directly at American power, institutional rot, religious hypocrisy, corporate greed, and the people who profit from keeping everyone exhausted and furious. Jourgensen has rarely been shy about announcing exactly what he thinks of the world, and Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery) gives him one final album-sized opportunity to unload. The record finds Ministry taking stock of those in charge, the damage they have caused, and whatever possibility remains for people trying to move forward together without surrendering their minds in the process. Jourgensen is equally direct about his decision to end the band. “I’m fucking done,” he says. “I’m proud of what I’ve accomplished. I’m amazed at the path that it’s taken, from With Sympathy to where we’re at today, and all points in between. It’s been quite a ride, but I’m completely at peace with the fact that it’s done. It’s time to herd goats.” It is a characteristically Jourgensen farewell. Ministry’s history has never followed a clean route, moving from the synth-pop framework of With Sympathy toward increasingly abrasive combinations of industrial electronics, metal, punk, samples, drum machines, and political invective. Along the way, the group built a catalogue whose influence spread through alternative rock, industrial metal, electronic music, and nearly every basement club willing to risk its speaker system. Burned Out surveys a planet apparently being administered by arsonists, war profiteers, algorithmic creeps, petty tyrants, and terminally online lunatics, while everybody else stares into the smoke wondering which official lie they are supposed to swallow today. Wars multiply, humanitarian disasters become background noise, the climate cooks, repression spreads, and domestic extremism crawls out of the basement wearing a flag. Beneath all that wreckage sits one stubborn plea: stand together before fear, division, and authoritarian power finish carving us into manageable pieces. The video turns the crisis into a parade of deranged animation, with Uncle Al planted at its center like the last sane man at the end of civilization, coat practically on, ready to abandon the madhouse before somebody asks him to save it. Watch below: Since beginning in 1981, Ministry has released 17 studio albums, 8 live releases, 8 side projects, tours across 5 continents, an autobiography, 2 documentaries, and at least 3 occasions on which Jourgensen received last rites. The survival stories became inseparable from the music, turning the band’s continued existence into a running argument against medical probability and professional caution. Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery) also closes part of the Ministry story by reconnecting Jourgensen with longtime member Paul Barker. Barker appears on the album’s final track, We’re Still Here, marking one last collaboration between two musicians whose work together helped define Ministry’s most widely celebrated period. The album also features Ministry’s current lineup, including guitarists Monte Pittman and Cesar Soto, bassist Paul D’Amour, sampler and synthesizer player John Bechdel, and drummer Pepe Clarke Magaña. Together, they provide the final formation behind a band that has spent 45 years treating complacency as an enemy and volume as a public service. Ministry’s final album, Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery), is out October 30 through Cleopatra Records. Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery) will be available in several formats including vinyl, CD, cassettes and digital, also including several vinyl variants and box sets: Green & Black Splatter LP Silver & Black Splatter LP Coke Bottle Green LP Box Set: Green Splatter LP, Picture LP, 7-inch, CD Box Set: Purple Marble LP, Picture LP, 7-inch, CD Fans can pre-save the digital album HERE and pre-order digital copies HERE, and find a new Ministry merch line HERE. Ministry will bring tracks from Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery) and other classic hits on the road in 2027 with an international goodbye tour. items.body: PUREST FORM’s latest single, ANIMAL, opens with electronic menace. A blunt industrial beat stomps into view, guitar slashes scrape across the machinery, and Story Beeson’s voice carries the command of somebody who has already located the emergency exit. The Los Angeles trio wanted “White Zombie meets Underworld,” which sounds on paper like a backstage argument at a 1997 festival, yet the combination proves remarkably natural. Beeson, guitarist and programmer Madi Woodward, and bassist Riley Oikawa-Dahlson bring hardcore discipline to music designed for bodies in motion. ANIMAL pivots between serrated riffs, fractured breakbeats, low-end pressure, and sudden structural swerves, but every turn feels purposeful. The track has muscle, sex, and a mean little grin. Its aggression never becomes gray sludge; there is too much rhythmic wit in the programming, too much snap in the bass, and too much pleasure in the collision between metal weight and acid-house momentum. There is also a refreshing lack of genre etiquette here; stylistic boundaries are treated as petty municipal ordinances, useful mainly for telling dull people where to stand, then barrel through them with the cheerful confidence of repeat offenders. Beeson’s performance supplies the volatile center. She delivers each line as though language has become a physical object requiring immediate disposal, shouting near the edge of collapse while retaining enough control to sharpen every phrase. Around her, Woodward’s guitar behaves less like decoration than a damaged power tool, while Oikawa-Dahlson keeps the track planted firmly enough for the electronics to lunge, buck, and misbehave. The video, directed by Beeson, extends the song’s argument into the realm of surveillance horror. “The video takes on the horror of surveillance,” says Beeson. “While using a lot of throwback technology, mostly to pay homage to its influence – Peter Christopherson’s video for Ministry’s Over The Shoulder, it very much intends to communicate how more modern technology is being used for violence against our communities and humanity as a whole. It fits with the concept of ANIMAL: whether the nature is sexual or simply a desire to exist, we deserve to have freedom and we must take that freedom back.” Watch the video for Animal below: That conviction also drives RESISTANCE, the six-track EP arriving September 4 through Dais Records. Written amid fires, displacement, ICE raids, and the grinding obscenity of late-stage capitalism, the record channels anger toward collective action rather than private despair. “Resistance, less of an idea, more of an absolute action that has to be taken,” asserts Beeson. ANIMAL makes that action feel immediate, physical, and dangerously enjoyable. Revolution may remain poorly organized, but PUREST FORM have at least supplied it with a better bassline. Listen to ANIMAL below and order the single here. items.body: Once all the papers get signed We lift you up on discount price You just have to make this sacrifice Every false prophet and messiah begins by telling the frightened that they have been chosen. The voice offers clarity, belonging, and the promise of a perfected self; only later come the contract, the price, and the surrender of everything that made the convert difficult to own. On Sacrifice, Southeast London industrial post-punk project The Pixel Rain sends that transaction through the age of algorithmic gurus, where charisma can pass for truth and transformation becomes a product. Sacrifice is the second single and opening track from The Pixel Rain’s forthcoming debut album, A Sense of Danger, currently scheduled for release in late October. Following Last, the song introduces the album’s post-apocalyptic frame through a society governed by power, authority, consumerism, and technological control. Sacrifice moves through a cyberpunk dream of deep bass, Kraftwerkian retro-computer pulses, and synth leads glowing with the sterile polish of a showroom terminal. Áron Siegler’s dusky voice maintains a close, controlled pressure throughout the verses, then surges through the chorus’s “So trust me,” landing somewhere between Brian Molko, Trent Reznor, and Paul Banks. Driving rhythms and industrial textures keep the track pushing ahead as the promise at its center grows steadily more predatory. The lyrics borrow the soothing vocabulary of cults, motivational seminars, and influencer culture. The prophet addresses his followers as “children,” while the parenthetical responses—“We’ll hold you” and “You know we leave no one behind”—resemble scripted affirmations designed to smother suspicion. A promise to remove self-doubt soon becomes permission to remove the self, with salvation reduced to paperwork, discount pricing, and the command, “You have to sell yourself tonight.” The final verse reveals what this digital saviour has wanted all along. “I prey on the void inside” turns an apparent confession of faith into an admission of appetite, before the closing line—“So we can eat you alive”—strips the sales pitch of its remaining benevolence. Siegler describes the false prophet behind the song: “‘Sacrifice’ started with the idea of modern-day false messiahs and how easily charisma can be mistaken for truth. As online platforms continue to blur the line between genuine guidance and performance, I found myself drawn to the psychology behind people who build influence by promising transformation. That idea felt like the perfect companion to the track’s cold, mechanical, electronic atmosphere.” The song’s science-fiction setting preceded its arrangement: “Like many of my songs, ‘Sacrifice’ started with a visual idea rather than a musical one. I was inspired by the worlds of Neuromancer and Cyberpunk 2077, and that atmosphere naturally led to a synth-heavy sound. From there, I mixed melodic influences from bands like Depeche Mode and Muse with the industrial pulse and textures of Nine Inch Nails and Ministry.” Created by Ádám Molnár, the accompanying lyric visualizer treats the viewer’s screen as the target of a computer virus. A digitized version of Siegler’s head becomes the infection’s persuasive face, addressing the viewer as the virtual machinery draws them further into its illusion. The polished interface connects the song’s false promises to the screens through which those promises now spread. Watch the visualizer for Sacrifice below: Sacrifice by The Pixel Rain is out via Bandcamp, Spotify, and all major digital platforms. A Sense of Danger is currently scheduled for release in late October. Listen to Sacrifice below, and order the single here. Sacrifice by The Pixel Rain Founded by Hungarian-born vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Áron Siegler, The Pixel Rain took shape within Southeast London’s underground and released a self-titled debut EP in 2023. Drawing from industrial rock, post-punk, synth-pop, and electronic music, Siegler balances guitar-led songwriting with layered production, dark atmospheres, and sharply defined melodies. A Sense of Danger extends that approach across songs concerned with power, authority, consumerism, and social unease, viewed through post-apocalyptic imagery and cold electronic machinery. items.body: Siouxsie and the Banshees released their third studio album, “Kaleidoscope,” on 1 August 1980 through Polydor Records. The album turns 46 this year. It arrived with a new lineup, drummer Budgie and guitarist John McGeoch replacing Kenny Morris and John McKay, who had abruptly left during the “Join Hands” tour, and it introduced synthesizers and drum machines to the band’s sound for the first time. The band recorded “Kaleidoscope” at Surrey Sound Studios in Leatherhead, the Coach House in Monmouth and Polydor Studios in London between January and May 1980, produced by Nigel Gray with Siouxsie and the Banshees. Siouxsie Sioux handled vocals along with guitar and synthesizer parts, Steven Severin played bass, guitar and synthesizer, and Budgie played drums and percussion; McGeoch contributed guitar, saxophone and keys, and Steve Jones added guitar on several tracks. The eleven-track album runs “Happy House,” “Tenant,” “Trophy,” “Hybrid,” “Clockface,” “Lunar Camel,” “Christine,” “Desert Kisses,” “Red Light,” “Paradise Place” and “Skin,” and was preceded by the singles “Happy House” and “Christine.” “Kaleidoscope” reached number 5 on the UK Albums Chart, the band’s highest chart position, and was later certified silver by the BPI. It streams on Spotify. About Siouxsie and the Banshees Siouxsie and the Banshees formed in London in 1976, when vocalist Siouxsie Sioux and bassist Steven Severin, part of the group of Sex Pistols followers known as the Bromley Contingent, put together an impromptu band to fill a slot at the 100 Club Punk Festival on 20 September 1976, playing a 20-minute improvisation with Marco Pirroni on guitar and Sid Vicious on drums. A settled lineup formed around Siouxsie, Severin, guitarist John McKay and drummer Kenny Morris, and Polydor signed the band in June 1978 after the single “Hong Kong Garden” reached the UK top ten. The band’s debut album, “The Scream,” followed on 13 November 1978, and “Join Hands” arrived in 1979. Two days into the tour for “Join Hands,” McKay and Morris abruptly left the band, and Siouxsie and the Banshees regrouped around new guitarist John McGeoch, formerly of Magazine, and new drummer Budgie, formerly of the Slits. This lineup of Siouxsie, Severin, McGeoch and Budgie recorded and released “Kaleidoscope” on 1 August 1980 through Polydor, reaching number 5 on the UK Albums Chart. The band followed it with “Juju” in 1981, which included the single “Spellbound,” and “A Kiss in the Dreamhouse” in 1982. McGeoch left the band in 1982, and the Cure’s Robert Smith joined as guitarist for the “A Kiss in the Dreamhouse” tour and the following two albums; John Valentine Carruthers then took over guitar for “Hyaena” (1984) and “Tinderbox” (1986), and the band released the covers album “Through the Looking Glass” in 1987. Guitarist Jon Klein joined for “Peepshow” (1988), which produced the US breakthrough single “Peek-a-Boo.” After a break during which Siouxsie and Budgie recorded as the Creatures, the band returned with “Superstition” (1991), led by the US hit single “Kiss Them for Me,” and toured as second headliners on the first Lollapalooza. “The Rapture,” produced with John Cale, followed in 1995 before Siouxsie and the Banshees disbanded in April 1996. “Kaleidoscope,” the album that introduced the McGeoch and Budgie-era lineup and the band’s electronic turn, turns 46 this year.

items.body: Suicide Commando, the Belgian electro-industrial project of Johan Van Roy, released its debut album Critical Stage on 1 August 1994 through the German label Off Beat. The CD turns 32 this year. The Suicide Sessions 1 (Critical Stage) by Suicide Commando “Critical Stage” contains 12 tracks, all written and performed by Van Roy, recorded and mixed by Eric Van Wonterghem at E.M.P.-studio. Cover design and layout came from Beyond > Mixed Data and Koen Cant. Track ten, “Where Do We Go From Here?”, carries voice and lyrics by Dirk Ivens, known from Dive, The Klinik and Absolute Body Control. Off Beat, a division of the German company Westcom, distributed the album through SPV GmbH. The original CD is out of print. The album can be streamed today via Bandcamp as part of “The Suicide Sessions 1 (Critical Stage)”, a 2011 reissue that restores the original twelve tracks alongside eleven bonus recordings. Out Of Line reissued “Critical Stage” separately on limited red and yellow vinyl in 2025. About Suicide Commando Johan Van Roy started experimenting with electronic music in Belgium in 1986 under the name Suicide Commando. His first tape followed two years later, and a track from it appeared on the vinyl compilation “Electronic.” After several more self-released tapes, Off Beat signed Van Roy, and Suicide Commando’s debut album, “Critical Stage,” followed in 1994. A second album, “Stored Images,” arrived in 1995 and included “See You in Hell.” In 1996, Van Roy marked the project’s tenth anniversary with the compilation “Contamination.” “Construct-Destruct” and its companion release “Reconstruction” followed in 1998, carrying the club tracks “Desire” and “Better Off Dead.” Van Roy co-founded the label Dependent in 1999. Suicide Commando’s next studio album, “Mindstrip” (2000), reached number one on the German Alternative Charts and was licensed for North America by Metropolis Records. Dependent also released the singles “Hellraiser” and “Comatose Delusion,” the EP “Love Breeds Suicide,” and the 2002 compilation “Anthology.” The 2003 album “Axis of Evil” was voted album of the year by the Deutsche Alternative Charts. “Bind, Torture, Kill” followed in 2006, preceded by the single “Godsend + Menschenfresser,” and reached number one on the DAC albums chart. Suicide Commando marked its 20th anniversary in 2007 with the “X20” boxset, including a remix disc, a “best of” disc, the “Fuck You Bitch” EP and the project’s first live DVD. In 2009, Van Roy signed with the German label Out Of Line, starting with the 7″ “Severed Head / Until We Die.” The album “Implements of Hell” followed in 2010, again licensed to Metropolis Records in the US. In 2011, Suicide Commando reissued its first three studio albums, “Critical Stage,” “Stored Images” and “Construct-Destruct,” as the six-CD box “The Suicide Sessions,” each remastered and paired with a disc of bonus and previously unreleased material. “When Evil Speaks” followed in 2013, led by the single “Attention Whore” and reaching number 47 on the German Media Control Charts. “Forest of the Impaled” (2017) included “The Pain That You Like,” a single featuring Jean-Luc De Meyer of Front 242 as guest vocalist, and reached number 28 on the same chart. Suicide Commando released the album “Goddestruktor” in 2022. For live shows, Van Roy performs alongside Torben Schmidt on keyboards and Mario Vaerewijck on drums. “Critical Stage,” the album that started the project’s studio discography, turns 32 on 1 August.

items.body: Hungarian artist István Gazdag has built a solid reputation within the EBM scene through his primary project, First Aid 4 Souls. A true workaholic, he is also active with side projects such as First Aid Tech. Two years ago, he released the outstanding debut album “Tech Under Your Skin” under this moniker. That impressive work is now followed by a new release featuring—once again—no fewer than 22 tracks. The influences remain largely unchanged. István Gazdag continues to experiment freely with a wide range of styles, moving from EBM—inevitably inviting comparisons to Front Line Assembly—to Tribal and Psy-Trance elements that occasionally evoke the spirit of Juno Reactor. Acid sequences emerge throughout the album, while guitar passages provide yet another subtle nod to the latter’s signature sound. Despite these obvious influences, First Aid Tech never comes across as derivative. Instead, the music feels like a seamless fusion of the various styles this sound guru effortlessly combines. There are no vocals, although carefully selected samples add extra depth and variety. The tracks frequently exude a menacing atmosphere that perfectly complements the album’s dark overall mood. Once again, Gazdag delivers a meticulously crafted production that merges boundless creativity with sophisticated, high-tech production values. To my ears, this new opus plays like the imaginary soundtrack to a “Matrix”-esque film. Above all, however, it stands as a brilliant, elaborate, and deeply immersive obscure Electro production. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Play My Game”: Play My Game by First Aid Tech About First Aid Tech First Aid Tech is a project of Hungarian electronic musician István Gazdag, who is also the driving force behind First Aid 4 Souls and Stahlgeist. First Aid 4 Souls, active since 2007, is known for its blend of industrial, EBM, dark ambient, trance, and new wave, often featuring guest vocalists. Stahlgeist deals in EBM that recalls the early years of Front Line Assembly and Wumpscut. Gazdag has performed and DJed under the First Aid Tech moniker for years, but the project’s first official release, a self-titled techno body EP featuring 4 tracks and 4 bonus remixes, only appeared on Alfa Matrix on December 4, 2023. The debut album, “Tech Under Your Skin,” followed on October 17, 2024. In a Side-Line interview, Gazdag described First Aid Tech’s sound DNA as rooted in 90s electronic music, citing Cabaret Voltaire, Orbital, Yello, Juno Reactor, LFO, Underworld, Empirion, and Future Sound Of London as reference points. The project now returns with its second full-length, “Back To Agartha.”

https://tfp-group.co.jp/love-bond/column/kaihitype-koi現在、成人の愛着スタイルを測る学術的な尺度としては「ECR(Experiences in Close Relationships)」やその改訂版「ECR-R」、Fraleyらによる「ECR-RS」などがあり、「不安」と「回避」という2軸で4タイプに分類する方式が主流です。出典: 「回避型」の特徴━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━複数の情報源に共通して挙げられている特徴をまとめると、以下のようになります。・一人の時間を強く好み、群れることを避ける・人に頼ることも、頼られることも苦手・感情表現が乏しく、自分の感情そのものに気づきにくい・関係が深まりそうになると自分から距離を置く、または関係を終わらせる・恋愛で好意を向けられると急に冷たくなる、連絡を絶つ・表面的には自立していて冷静に見えるが、内面では孤独感や空虚感を抱えている・過去や自分の感情に向き合うことを頑なに避ける・子ども時代の記憶があいまいなことが多い出典: https://katsushikabashi.jp/article/avoidant-attachment-style/岡田尊司氏の著書「回避性愛着障害」では、感情を強く揺さぶられる写真を一瞬見せて理解するまでの時間を計測する実験が紹介されており、回避型の人は感情を喚起する写真の理解に時間がかかる(=感情への反応が鈍い)という結果が示されています。この傾向は自然の風景や無機物の写真には見られなかったとされています。出典: https://coconala.com/blogs/2307087/319522(岡田尊司「愛着障害~子供時代を引きずる人々~」からの引用紹介)━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━■3. 英語圏での分類：dismissive-avoidant(拒絶回避型)━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━英語圏では回避型は主に「dismissive-avoidant(拒絶回避型)」と呼ばれ、以下のような特徴が整理されています。・極端な自己完結性・独立性・親密になることへの抵抗、コミットメントの回避・表面的な会話で終わらせようとする傾向・長期的な関係より短期的・カジュアルな関係を好む傾向があるという研究結果もある・パートナーへの依存(interpersonal dependence)や信頼のスコアが低い・失恋時の苦痛が(特に男性で)比較的軽いという研究結果もある出典: https://www.simplypsychology.org/dismissive-avoidant-attachment-style-signs-how-to-heal.html出典:
