"Written and recorded during pregnancy and early motherhood, Rose Keeler-Schaffeler's album draws inspiration from the earliest forms of human communication: coos, cries, sighs and instinctive vocalisations that precede language yet already contain the seeds of music. Best known as Keel Her, the cult DIY songwriter, producer and NTS Radio DJ whose fiercely independent body of work helped define a generation of bedroom
items.body:
Rose Keeler-Schaffeler's second release 'Universal Language' via Magic Hollow.

"Written and recorded during pregnancy and early motherhood, Rose Keeler-Schaffeler's album draws inspiration from the earliest forms of human communication: coos, cries, sighs and instinctive vocalisations that precede language yet already contain the seeds of music.

Best known as Keel Her, the cult DIY songwriter, producer and NTS Radio DJ whose fiercely independent body of work helped define a generation of bedroom pop, Rose reveals a strikingly different side of her musical practice here. Produced by Daniel O'Sullivan, Universal Language places the human voice at its centre, treating it not as a vehicle for lyrics but as the raw material from which music, language and relationships emerge.

With the exception of a handful of bass vocal parts performed by O'Sullivan, every voice heard on the album is Rose's own.

Across twelve meticulously composed pieces, layered vocal arrangements intertwine with subtle electronics, tape manipulation, synthesizers and understated drum machines. At times the music evokes the luminous purity of medieval sacred music; elsewhere voices dissolve into hazy ambient textures or unfold through hypnotic loops that blur the distinction between singer, choir and atmosphere.

The album was recorded during the first year of her son’s life. Many of its melodic contours and vocal gestures were inspired directly by his earliest sounds. His pre-linguistic attempts at communication became compositional material, guiding Rose towards a deeper exploration of the voice at its point of origin.

Deeply personal yet reaching towards something universal, Universal Language is a meditation on the human voice: our first instrument, our first language and our first experience of belonging."

items.body:
NWW cruise to Cuba via Cooloorta with Señor Coconut, Andrew Liles, Colin Potter, Matt Waldron & Diarmuid MacDiarmada in tow, on a 2CD expansion of their ludic ’95 LP

Regular cited among NWW’s daftest, most sinisterly whimsical, but also creepy, the original ‘Alice The Goon’ comprised their fruity yet uneasy ’95 homage to Pérez Prado, The King of the Mambo, and a lurid Popeye cartoon, backed with a signature slice of PCP-dosed soundscaping, ‘Prelude to Alice the Goon’ harking to their earliest trips, replete with personnel of that era including David Tibet, Diana Rogerson, and Sarah Dawson, alongside Steven Stapelton and others. 

Both original works are included on this massively expanded 2CD edition, encompassing Diarmuid MacDiarmada’s ‘I Yam What I Yam Intro’ channelling Popeye via Stars on 45 (Pints), and his tripper, 12 min mix ‘And That's All That I Yam Conclusion / Confusion’, plus a standout ‘Coconut Mix’ by Uwe Schmidt’s Señor Coconut, subtly spiced with glitches and hallucinatory electronics for properly uneasy listening. Along with the ’Soliloquy For Lilith’-like drone haunting of ‘Psuedoacacia’, and Matthew Waldron’s crawl-pace, 45’ rabbit hole screw of the ‘Alice the Goon’, it’s a real one for the sky lickers.

items.body:
Legendary pianist John Tilbury (founding member of free improv titans AMM), captured playing piano, clavichord & organ at home as he approached his 90th birthday this year, ending his recording career with a wonderful, generous set that also includes selected, notable archival works. The set covers everything from Elizabethan songbooks to contemporary compositions by pals including Mark R. Taylor and Catherine Kontz plus archive recordings of pieces by Christian Wolff, Morton Feldman and others, an organ improvisation with Keith Rowe, and much more. As the label perfectly put it - Tilbury is a giant in the history of contemporary, improvised and experimental music -  it’s a real pleasure to have a final document spanning generations, and eras, of his practice. 

From the foreword to the included booklet:

“In 2018 John Tilbury became reluctant to take on more concerts. He lives in Deal on the Kent coast, 80 miles from London, and doesn’t have a car, so, although he was still in demand as a performer, at the age of 82, he decided to end his performing career. When I heard this, I asked whether - if I came to him - he would still be happy to be recorded at home. He said yes, and from then until spring 2026 I travelled to Deal every 6 or 9 months to record John playing piano and clavichord in the lean-to extension at the back of the terrace house where he and his wife Janice live.

We recorded whatever John wanted to play at the time, and so assembled an unusual and varied collection of recordings ranging from pieces from Elizabethan songbooks to new compositions sent by old friends from Scratch Orchestra days. Sometimes, if John was tired or in pain, we didn’t record very much, and the visits became as much a social thing as a recording session - and it was always very enjoyable to talk with John and Janice about music and politics, and hear stories about John’s past and his many musical friends.

In early 2026 – around the time of his 90th birthday - John decided that if we carried on much longer, he’d no longer be able to do justice to the music he was playing, and that we should stop. The original idea – insofar as we had one - was to release a selection of what we’d recorded as an album, but once we started listening back to everything, John suggested that we also include some archive recordings, dating from as far back as the 1970’s. So began a process of discussion, whittling down the many things we could have included, until we agreed on the contents of the four CDs in this box set, which effectively marks the end of John’s recording career.”

Simon Reynell, May 2026

"Kel Tamacheq” is years in the making, a self produced DIY album, recorded in the small studios of the Malian capital over the past few years.Carrying on in the tradition of assouf, the Northern Malian style of Tuareg guitar popularized b
items.body:
Tuareg blues band Amana de Kidal, so named for their north Saharan home town, call for unity between Mali’s myriad ethnicities across a joyful and driving album of pentatonic riffs and rooted grooves.

“Studio album from Bamako-based Tuareg band Amanar de Kidal. "Kel Tamacheq” is years in the making, a self produced DIY album, recorded in the small studios of the Malian capital over the past few years.Carrying on in the tradition of assouf, the Northern Malian style of Tuareg guitar popularized by artists like Tinariwen, Amanar pushes the sound forward into tight upbeat groove and kinetic rhythms, reflecting the rich diversity of Mali and the energy of the capital. 

The band takes its name from their hometown Kidal, a remote outpost deep in the Saharan mountains of the far North. Led by singer/songwriter Ahmed Ag Kaedy, the band Amanar has spent the past 15 years dispersed, with Kaedy making his home in Bamako.

The title, meaning “Tuareg People” in Tamasheq, carries with it a message: a call for unity among the scattered community. Recorded with musicians from across Mali’s many ethnic communities, “Kel Tamasheq” is not just a personal vision, but a sketch for a country at peace. "Among the Tuareg, some are with Mali, some are with the rebels, some are with the Jihadists”, Kaedy says. “The spirit of the album is to say: our misfortune is the source of our division. It's an album driven by Tuareg identity. If we can remember who we are, and let it guide us, we will never lose the road."

items.body:
Unmissable reissue of Valya Hooi’s standout debut, an immaculately frayed conception of dubwise dream-pop from the same Aussie quarters that gave us HTRK/Jonnine, CS + Kreme, F Ingers...

Valya's first record ‘Untitled’ was originally issued by Altered States Tapes in 2019 (the same year as her song-writing credit on ‘I Don’t Seem Myself Tonight’ from Jonnine’s ’Super Natural’ EP), and has somehow managed to evade our radar until now, when she’s making a fairly big ping in our world.

Working economically with her own vocals, plus guitar, keyboards, and slivers of clarinet supplied by Tarquin Manek (F Ingers, LST), the results can’t help but remind us to aspects of Laila Sakini or Teresa Winter’s music that we hold dearly - namely the reverb-laden vocals and drowsily psychedelic, daydreaming appeal - but also tend toward a sort of sublime, grown-up bedroom chamber darkness understandably shared with her peer Jonnine, and the low-key grooving suss of CS + Kreme, or even Mica Levi at her most strung out. 

An incredible album.

items.body:
Epic 16 hour François Bayle retrospective, an unparalleled document of the key C.20th electro-acoustic and concrète pioneer and director of the hugely influential GRM institution from 1966-1997, where he was instrumental in bringing the Acousmonium speaker array and INA-GRM label to life, among many important, enduring innovations

This 10 year reissue of ’50 Ans d’Acousmagique’ joins INA-GRM’s quintessential boxsets of Pierre Schaeffer, Pierre Henry, Parmegiani, Radigue, and Xenakis in a rare, stellar microcosm of works by twentieth century groundbreakers. At 16 hrs long, and including 228 tracks, it offers a comprehensive overview of François Bayle’s unfathomable catalogue of work between 1972-2012. During this time Bayle was pivotal in altering perceptions of music’s materiality and purpose at the most fundamental and philosophic levels through his work in developing the Acousmonium diffusion system - an “orchestra of loudspeakers” which has become key to the GRM’s facilities in Paris - as well as supporting technological developments (Syter, GRM Tools, Midi Formers, Acousmographe) which are vital to his own remarkable compositions, and his endeavours organising radio broadcasts and events. 

Deeply informing and paralleling the history of recorded electronic music during its formative golden years, Bayle’s recordings render an embarrassment of riches for the discerning and explorative listener and historians of vanguard C.20th music. Between the flighty electro-acoustic staging of his avian dreams on ’72’s ‘Trois Rêves D'oiseau’ to the sensually lathered cosmic delirium of 1978-80’s ‘Erosphère’ works, to his beguiling latter tributes to his tutors at the Paris Conservatoire and Darmstadt summer courses, Messiaen and Stockhausen; the overwhelming scope of Bayle’s work, and thus the boxset, is brought into clearer focus by its chronological sequencing, offering a logical pathway thru his incredible projections of imagination.

It bears reflection that figures such as François Bayle created, and then opened, doors of perception for music in the past century that have come to mirror and shape the soundsphere we now inhabit. His innovations in sound spatialisation and the embrace of an acoustic unknown, or acousmagique, underline some of the most fascinating expressions of pathos thru art in our lifetimes, and this boxset is more than enough to send heads reeling into deep time for eons to come.

items.body:
Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot.

Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. OK the formula is there, but Chris Carter’s ‘Spaces Between’ (1980) and his CTI jam ‘Dancing Ghosts’ got there a couple of years before Singh, at the very least, and neither really inform the genius of Phuture and co a few years later. In any event, ‘Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’ is just an incredibly fruity boost to any club, revolving 10 hypnotic, pulsating jams closer to early Irdial (say, Aqua Regia’s ‘Hot Love’) than owt from the Chi. 

Taking a minute away from knocking out Bollywood scores and leading his wedding band covering popular songs, Singh would land upon a stroke of genius with ‘Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’, finding the sweetspot between prevailing hi-NRG disco and millennia of raga traditions that patently transcended the sum of their parts more than 40 years later. It sounds very much of its time, rather than the stripped back linearity of later acid house, evidenced in the florid keyboard urges of ‘Raga Bhupali’, transposing a steamy sort of club canter to somewhere even more humid.

A real club evergreen, suck it and see.

Armed with a refreshed, rugged palette and hunger for tuffer techno, Phillip Sollmann marks some 30 years of fuelling the ‘floor with the ‘Mirror Phase EP’, which escalates in increasingly hard-edged turns from the title tune’s harmonic Berlin-Via-Detroit techno to sludgier acid techno teeming with strange voices in ‘FS1R’, into full Motor City-style flight, a la ‘Landcruising’-era Carl Craig, on ‘Unity Grain’, and the brisk, tweaked-out trot of ’Slip’, which builds to a glorious posh trance peak.

items.body:
Wiry, tart, cold, minimal wave shrapnel from original early ‘80s upswell of DIY machine music...

“40 years after its creation, MOß GARTEN – Sekvensstyrd 1981–1986 arrives as a compelling double vinyl LP, diving deep into the early Swedish DIY electronic scene. Inspired by pioneers such as Kraftwerk, Cabaret Voltaire, John Foxx, and The Human League, Mikael Isaksson developed a distinct sound situated between minimal electronics, industrial, synth wave, and experimental sound art. At its core was the sequencer: pulsing, programmed structures forming the backbone of dense, often hypnotic compositions.

Working initially with his cousin Jan or friend Thomas and later evolving into a largely one-man project, recordings were made on cassette tapes and in improvised studios—often under time pressure, frequently recorded and mixed within just a few hours. These very limitations gave the tracks their raw and immediate character. Pieces like “Moderna Kvinnor,” “Soon Soon,” “Ensam,” and “Music From The Border” exemplify the uncompromising, sequence-driven (“sekvensstyrd”) approach that defined this era.

Using an arsenal of analog synthesizers, early sequencers, and drum machines, the project created music that feels at once cold, mechanical, and deeply emotional. Sekvenssytrd 1981–1986 is more than a collection of archival recordings—it is a vivid document of a time when electronic music was conceived as a radical and deeply personal form of expression.”

The reviews below offer a glimpse of just some of his production over the first half of this year. See part 1 here . Udo Schindler and Andreas Willers – Analytical Pre-Summer Retreat (FMR, 2026) Analytical Pre-Summer Retreat captures Schindler (tenor sax, e-flat clarinet, piccolo flute, and cornet) with Berlin improvisor Andreas Willers (guitar and devices) at a live date at St
items.body: German multi-instrumentalist Udo Schindler has been recording and releasing music relentlessly over the last few years. The reviews below offer a glimpse of just some of his production over the first half of this year. See part 1 here . Udo Schindler and Andreas Willers – Analytical Pre-Summer Retreat (FMR, 2026) Analytical Pre-Summer Retreat captures Schindler (tenor sax, e-flat clarinet, piccolo flute, and cornet) with Berlin improvisor Andreas Willers (guitar and devices) at a live date at Studio+Atelier SCHINDLER in Krailing/Munich in 2025. The two had previously collaborated on 2022’s STORM without WIND and a 2023 trio session with Eric Zwang Eriksson titled Cassiber Complex_Unconditioned Sounds In A Box. As with the other, this one shows range, but a different range than the more restrictively acoustic outings reviewed above. Here one hears how electric Schindler’s trills and flutters can sound, and Willers, with over forty years of electro-acoustic collaboration under his belt, is the person to bring that out. He veers from shreds and electronic chaos to simple repeating clusters and other rummaging to prickly vines with a Scandinavian free rock sensibility a la Tellef Øgrim, Gunnar Backmann, and their ilk. A gritty and textured set that is as much about Schindler’s arsenal (including some nice trumpet work) as it is about Willers’ clattery fretwork. Analytical Pre-Summer Retreat is available via the arc-musik website: https://arch-musik.de/project/analytical-pre-summer-retreat/ . Udo Schindler, Harald Kimmig, Eric Zwang Eriksson – Imprints of Experiences (Creative Sources, 2026) With a total of three members, Imprints of Experiences captures the largest unit of the releases reviewed here, and its sound is correspondingly (and comparatively) full. Schindler deploys a range of instruments, some heard before (clarinets, cornet, saxophone) and one (b-flat tubax) unique to this recording. Harald Kimmig meanwhile contributes an energetic violin and Eric Zwang Eriksson, an array of prattling percussion. Playing live over two nights in Munich in 2024, the trio offers quite a range of sounds. Schindler does his thing, screeching, torquing, huffing, and, now, even singing through an array of horns. Kimmig and Eriksson, however, really distinguish this release. Eriksson and Schindler have collaborated frequently over the last half-decade, and the resulting concordance shows especially in the quieter segments, when Eriksson matches Schindler’s clucks and clicks with a concerted pitter patter of his own. Kimmig, who has a shorter history with Schindler, can also tap raindrops and rustling foliage, but shows he can also drive the trio out of these moments through his sharp and shimmering tremolo, at which points Schindler starts to stretch out into more frenzied spaces. This may be less rambunctious than some other releases, but it is no less probing, and even more entrancing. And some of that pull should be attributed specially to Eriksson and his controlled but curious rummaging. It lays a calm but spumy sediment that gives bubbly rise to the harmonics that fill out the wider sound. Imprints of Experiences is available on CD and as a download on bandcamp. Imprints of Experiences by Udo Schindler, Harald Kimmig & Eric Zwang Eriksson PS: I had originally intended to review Schindler’s 2026 releases up through June, however quickly I realized that was a fool’s errand. For those interested, this year he also released albums with Andrea Centazzo and Harnik on Itcus, Nicola Hein and Nikolaus Neuser on Creative Sources, and Flo Stoffner and Michael Wintsch on arc-musik. By the time this review runs, there will likely be others, as well. Happy listening. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

After consulting the Attorney-General’s Chambers, police administered stern warning
items.body:
Two members of Massive Attack have been issued stern warnings and barred from re-entering Singapore following the band’s concert at The Star Theatre on 29 July.

In a joint statement issued on 31 July, the Singapore Police Force and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) said two band members had been investigated for supporting a political cause and displaying a Palestinian flag during the performance.

After consulting the Attorney-General’s Chambers, police administered stern warnings to both men for offences under Section 3 of the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act and Section 16 of the Public Order Act.

Both members will be banned from entering Singapore again. As a result of the entry ban, IMDA said it would not approve any future applications for Massive Attack to perform in the country.

The agency is separately investigating possible breaches of several conditions attached to the concert’s licence, including one prohibiting “the display of flags in support of any causes”. IMDA said it would take the necessary action once its investigations had concluded.

During the concert, Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall were seen holding up a Palestinian flag as the audience cheered. Del Naja also said “Free Palestine”, before members of the crowd independently took up the chant. The band also told the crowd that they had pulled a song from the intended setlist due to “local laws.”

Singapore prohibits the public display of foreign national emblems without a permit or exemption. Those convicted may be fined up to S$500, imprisoned for up to six months, or both.

Police said they took a serious view of acts that could potentially affect Singapore’s racial and religious harmony. They also urged residents and visitors not to “import foreign politics”, saying this could undermine social cohesion and the rule of law.

Concert promoter Lushington Entertainments previously said it would “fully cooperate with the relevant authorities as required”.

items.body: The soulless age of the Hollywood blockbuster, rife with CGI and A.I., has left viewers nostalgic for the golden age of cinema, when a widescreen epic meant months of set building and thousands of extras, but a small, intimate picture with a compelling story could still become a runaway smash. Ori Kaplan & Lihu Melamed‘s Reverie recalls the film scores of this era, focusing on the timbres of the 1960s and 70s while unfolding like a reel of greatest themes. At various junctures, one may think of a love story, a car chase, or a desert crossing; the high drama of a western, the tension of a spy film, or even the snappy banter of a Blaxploitation flick. The cover implies a weirdness, a readiness to experiment, the courage to walk deep into a haunted glade, well aware of the danger. While the album is offered as an LP, it would also work well as a series of 45s. The saxophone groove of opener “Merveille” is enhanced by rustic surf guitar and psychedelic flute, all nudged forward by the drums: a happy opening scene in which the early characters are introduced. One can imagine this as a double A-sided single along with “Nuna,” which is not only brassy in timbre, but in tone, confident as a Times Square pimp in the neon era. See how he struts, puffing on a cigar, not a care in the world, while the Vietnam War rages on the other side of the sea. “The Stroll” and “Shangri-La” ease the drama down, more like Central Park on a summer day. The lovers-to-be are walking arm in arm, taking time to smell the flowers, laughing at each other’s little jokes, unaware that they will be lovers, but we know; we’ve seen the trailer. When the choir sings, it sings for them. The title “Obelisk” recalls “2001,” but the music is more like a suede jacket with patches on the arms, a book tucked under the arm, a cappuccino in a cafe. Each piece has its own distinct vibe; one writes the scenes in one’s head as one listens. While each stems from a different (imaginary) film, all are playing at the same theatre on a glorious festival weekend. The comfort of the organic notes matches the nostalgia for 8mm film; with delight, one remembers that one has not yet seen every classic film, which means that wonders still await. Even when one has seen a classic film, one may have done so when much younger, absorbing the score without noticing it; Reverie calls attention to the evocative power of sound. The diptych “Lost Soul” and “Soul Found” brings the point home. The first begins with conversational bustle, as at the start of a screening, and a lonesome yearning; the second, a 48 second coda, operates as the end credits. The movie is over, and we already want to see it – and hear it – again. (Richard Allen)

items.body: The drums lead everything on “Problems”. Femi Koleoso of Ezra Collective produced it, and he built the song the way he plays, from the rhythm out. Two drummers and two bassists lock together first, a percussionist works the gaps, and the horns of Egypt 80 land on top with their baritone saxophones sitting low. Seun Kuti has led his father Fela‘s band since 1997, and he sings the way he always has, hoarse and declamatory, going straight at the argument. Kabaka Pyramid answers from Kingston, a Grammy winner whose roots-reggae cadence carries a hip-hop swing. Between them the track moves between Lagos and Kingston, which Seun hears as a reunion across the diaspora. “Problems” deals with everyday struggle, the grind Seun sums up in three words, “hard like Sudoku”, a puzzle with no way out. The song is about getting through the chaos and staying on your feet under daily pressure, and Seun aims it at everyone rather than one country or class. It came out on 29 July as the B-side to “Na Dem“, the Tom Morello collaboration Seun first played at Coachella, and the two come together on a 7″ through Django Music in September. items.body: Review by kev rowland — As one may ascertain from the title, Aether are back with their third album in fairly quick succession, continuing in the similar excellent vein established with their 2024 album, 'Trans-Neptunian Objects'. It is again fully instrumental, apart from a recitative interlude by Claudio Milano (Nichelodeon) on "Vogon", and was recorded live in the studio, with the songs themselves developed on themes discovered during rehearsals and improvisations undertaken during 2025. It is the same line-up as on the previous releases, namely Andrea Ferrari (guitars, keyboards), Andrea Grumelli (fretless bass), Andrea Serino (Fender Rhodes, keyboards) and Matteo Ravelli (drums, electronics) and somehow, they are seamlessly combining music from genres as diverse as ambient/New Age, symphonic, classical and jazz to create something which at times is delicate yet at others is incredibly powerful indeed.Depending on what track I am listening to I find myself moving more to the keyboards, or possible the strident piano, or the fretless bass, or the controlled percussive elements which are much more than "just" drums, or the careful use of guitar, or even the wider use of space and silence. One never knows where the album is going to lead, which is what makes it so interesting, as it varies so much but somehow everything is connected, while the introduction of flute (Rosarita Crisafi) on a few of the tracks is inspired. Just now I was thinking how much this music made me think of a river then looked at the press release to confirm I had some information correct, and they also describe the track I was listening to ("Panta Rei") as a raging river, so we must be aligned. This is one where the guitar slowly makes its entrance felt, becoming more dominant throughout, yet it is the combination of all instruments which makes this such a standout piece.I was not the biggest fan of their debut, but they found their feet with the second and this is another absolute delight which is progressive in its truest sense and stands apart from the crowd. Well worthy of investigation.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A sextet featuring two guitarists, a keyboardist-composer whose keyboard sounds are worth ten people's efforts (no exaggeration), and, to top it all off, Bobby Previte on drums, could only be a group truly worthy of the name. And this holds true in the best sense of musical politics, as The President's second album solidified a modern fusion sound, blending blues, a touch of Krautrock, and minimalism, while the core sound of the opening track, "Hearts Are Broken," even evokes a desert-like atmosphere before branching out into the various facets the band goes on to explore.Philip begins to reveal that distinctive compositional touch of Horvitz, one that defies classification because it is meant to be felt rather than understood, with its sounds... and silences, and those pauses that stand out just as the melody decides to start up again. Like the white spaces in a painting, they are not placed there by chance.There is a distinctly rural, bluesy guitar feel; when the electric guitar enters to jam, it contrasts with Doug Wieselman's saxophone, which had begun in the style of a standard, creating a sound that is thoroughly contemporary American."Ride the Wide Streets" pumps out a rhythm like a mechanical lung; its composition seems destined to be a radio hit, in an ideal world where distorted guitar dances with atonal sax and the drums never stop playing. It is a near-feverish anthem that, with a steady cadence, leads us into "Our Hands of Water," driven by Wayne's keyboards, which arrive sounding almost otherworldly. The percussion has an almost Eastern feel, while the distortion gives it an even more jungle-like quality."Clear the Bridge" stretches the notes until they become rubbery, first the guitar, then the keyboard, rendering the musical staff malleable and melting it down until it aligns with the album's central premise. It evokes a desert crisscrossed by roads lined with endless, receding poles that repeat endlessly, stretching to the point where the horizon blurs into the landscape.Wayne is, among other things, a man of a thousand sounds on the keyboards; this work differs from his collaborations with John Zorn, as here he has the freedom to explore wherever his compositional mind takes him, a blend of the American past, classical music, and the avant-garde. The groove established by Bobby Previte, combined with Elliott Sharp's saxophone and guitar work, is truly incomparable. Likewise, Dave Tronzo's slide playing transports the listener, such as on "Andre's Mood," alongside Doug Wieselman. Interestingly, Elliott Sharp employs highly progressive scales that evoke the style of David Torn and his work with Bill Bruford.Andre's Mood takes a turn toward the psychedelic and even the funky; it really takes flight, with the sextet's lineup allowing for studio improvisation that captured the energy of a live performance. It was a prolific era for their songwriting, as 3 Crows demonstrates, with each track possessing its own distinct personality and sound, despite the album's overall cohesion. That personality is enviable; the band's signature style is unmistakable throughout. 3 Crows is modern and daring; it reminds me of The New Age, a Michael Tolkin film whose soundtrack, despite dating back to 1994, captured the pulse of the world during that early-90s period (which had actually begun in 1989). The album eventually builds to "A Bad Dream", the penultimate and longest track, which unfolds almost like a suite, fully developing the musical ideas presented earlier. This second album is warm and energetic, unlike its equally brilliant predecesor, and stands as a testament to the trio; perhaps that is precisely what makes it unique. Each of the three albums was distinct, despite sharing a common sound.The interplay of the two guitars and the saxophone shapes the melody of "A Bad Dream," giving it a classic feel as its echoes fade into the wind. Meanwhile, "Wish the Children Would Come on Home" is another exercise in repetition, reminiscent of Herbie Hancock's work with the Headhunters in the 70s, yet the harmonica lends it a twilight atmosphere that is unmistakably postmodern, heralding the arrival of something... though exactly what remains unclear. That enigmatic spirit, characteristic not only of Horvitz but of John Zorn's entire New York school, is palpable here on this essential album for understanding the early 90s scene.

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — In the summer of 1976 an album appeared in Italian shops with almost nothing to declare: a single laminated sleeve, a cover image suspended somewhere between deep space and an esoteric treatise on the mind, a name that sounded like a machine rather than a band, and no credits at all. Everything was signed by a certain Mr. Elektriktus. Italy at the time was living through its most feverish years, between political tension, terrorism and a cultural revolution that pushed musicians towards jazz, avant-garde and open experiment as a form of statement. In that climate, a record of pure electronics with no faces attached was not eccentric; it was almost a natural gesture of anonymity. Decades later the mask came off: behind Elektriktus stood Andrea Centazzo, born in Udine in 1948, percussionist and composer, already a veteran of free jazz and of collaborations with Giorgio Gaslini. The name itself is a small confession, a fusion of "electronic" and "Ictus", the trio and later the label that would accompany his whole career. The choice of PDU was less accidental than it looks: Mina's label was also the Italian distributor of Ohr and Kosmische Kuriere, so the German cosmic current entered the country through that very door.The album was born in a small home studio in the hills of Friuli, built with money earned on the road, equipped with a four track TEAC and a handful of primitive analogue keyboards. Centazzo composed, played and overdubbed everything himself, with the mixdown finished at the PDU Basilica Studios in Milan. The only guest is Franco Feruglio, whose double bass surfaces on "First Wave" and instantly changes the temperature of the record, dragging the sequencers back towards the improvisational world Centazzo came from. The result is not an imitation of Tangerine Dream or Klaus Schulze, and it would be lazy to file it that way. The closer reference is Conrad Schnitzler, or the early Roberto Cacciapaglia, or Hydrus, another PDU child: music built on pulse and pattern rather than on cathedral-sized drones. What makes it Italian is the physicality, the hand of a percussionist that never fully disappears behind the machines, the sense that these frequencies are being played rather than programmed. There is also a discreet narrative frame: a door, an engine starting, a departure at dawn, a flight, a return at dusk, an engine switched off. Eight pieces, three on the first side and five on the second, that behave like the stations of a single journey.- Frequencer Departure: Flying At Day-Break: the door slams, the engine turns over, and the sequencers take control with a hardness that still surprises today. After the first minutes the grip loosens and the piece opens into a hovering, atmospheric drift, with bass and percussion gradually giving flesh to the pulse. The most confident opening statement on the album.- First Wave: the heart of the record. Feruglio's double bass improvises against the electronic grid, and for five minutes krautrock and free jazz share the same room without arguing. Nothing else in Italian electronics of those years sounds quite like this.- Power Allucination (spelled that way on the original sleeve): the harshest passage, closer to tape music and musique concr�te than to cosmic reverie. Abrasive, deliberately uncomfortable, and essential to the balance of the whole.- Second Wave: the shortest track, a breath between two more demanding pieces, built on a simple cyclical figure that dissolves before it can settle.- Implosion: the title is honest. Layers accumulate and then collapse inward, with a claustrophobic quality that recalls the more psychological side of the German school rather than its interstellar side.- Third Wave: the most Schulze-like moment, brooding synthesizer lines expanding slowly over a patient sequence. The place where the album finally allows itself some warmth.�- Flying At Sunset: the return leg, more melodic and more resigned, light falling rather than rising. Short, and all the more effective for it.- Frequencer Arrival: the circle closes. The engine returns, the motion stops, and the journey ends exactly where it began, which was clearly the intention from the first groove.Electronic Mind Waves sold almost nothing. The lack of promotion and the end of Centazzo's contract buried it, and for years it survived only as a rumour among collectors, before the AMS and Ictus reissue of 2007 and the Wah Wah vinyl edition of 2011 brought it back into circulation. Listening to it now, its limits are audible: the four track origin leaves a certain thinness in the upper registers, a few passages sound more like laboratory notes than finished compositions, and the record occasionally seems to be discovering its own language while it plays. Yet that is precisely its charm. This is the sound of a jazz percussionist walking alone into unfamiliar territory, with modest equipment and immodest ambition, and returning with something genuinely his own. It remains one of the few Italian records of the seventies that can stand next to the German cosmic canon without asking permission, and one of the most quietly adventurous artefacts of the whole peninsular scene. Not a masterpiece, but an excellent album and a small act of courage. 4/5.

items.body: Review by vmagistr — Between 1973 and 1979 ? the years spanning the period between his departure from Deep Purple and his joining Rainbow ? Roger Glover experienced what was perhaps the most creative period of his life. He no longer had to be "just" a bassist (albeit in a top-notch hard rock band) and was able to channel his musical talent in many different directions. With his bass (or synthesizer), he occasionally did some guest studio work, but primarily he produced as if his life depended on it ? Nazareth, Elf, Rory Gallagher, and Judas Priest knew exactly who they were dealing with. He also found time for his own projects, most of which featured his original compositions. He enlisted many of his friends to help create the 1974 art-rock or pop-rock album (depending on how you view the music) "Butterfly Ball"; on the studio album Elements, released four years later, he made do with a smaller, tighter lineup.It's hard to say whether Glover ever embarked on a more ambitious recording in his career. Progressive suites featuring a prominent orchestral role used to be all the rage ? but not in 1978, when the increasingly popular punk scene was all the rage. Instead of rebellion and defiance, the bassist set out to compose a tribute to the four elements that surround us: earth, fire, water, and air. The music he created is somewhat in the spirit of some of Rick Wakeman's 1970s solo albums, except that here, strings take center stage instead of the ubiquitous keyboards. Rock fans, don't worry ? it's still a driving and catchy affair.I probably enjoy the opening track, The First Ring Made of Clay, the most ? in part because it has (along with the closing Finale) the only vocal track on the album. You'll find everything here ? a fantastic atmosphere, powerful melodies, and enchanting female vocals. Glover isn't afraid to shift between moods and genres, so in the following tracks you'll encounter, for example, a trotting piece peppered with instrumental solos (The Next Ring of Fire), a dreamy stroll through a blooming garden (The Third Ring's Watery Flow), or a repetitive raga (The Fourth Ring with the Wind).If you're a fan of the music of the aforementioned Rick Wakeman, Mike Oldfield, or perhaps the early '70s Moody Blues, this music might grab you. However, if you value Roger Glover primarily as a "hard-hitting" bassist, Elements might not be the album for you. It's by no means a groundbreaking recording, but rather a successful attempt by an ambitious artist to raise the bar a bit in terms of his creative abilities.

items.body: Review by AWizardATrueAimee — The Form of the Good is not an album I visit all that often but I still get back into at least once every 12 months or so since I'll suddenly have a need that I'm required to fulfill. Dan Britton is one of those individuals where I did my best to retain his name after hearing his contributions to the genre and seeing some of his live efforts back in his NEARfest days. Deluge Grander isn't my favorite band in the world but I think it's important to reflect back to the days when this album came out. Progressive rock certainly wasn't dead but it wasn't something that most would stumble across. It felt then more like a relic of a genre, leaving a lot of listeners to either revel in the past or stop listening to anything new. Needless to say, Deluge Grander was a cold glass of water in the midst of a sparse desert at the time and I feel like The Form of the Good is one of those albums that hit the moment perfect.Before the Common Era starts things off with a fantastic visceral tone that's sweet but grandiose. The Tree Factory has a track title that implies things are about to get fun and it certainly doesn't disappoint once it kicks in around the 2 minute mark. Admittedly, the album does have a bit of a monotone sound because of the recording but on this track I feel it makes the drums a bit more punchy and blunt. This band certainly knows how to build a song before letting out a fantastic release almost every time and The Tree Factory is a great place to hear what I'm trying to say.Common Era Caveman continues along what's starting to feel more and more like a repeated concept. Britton really is a professional in his craft and hearing his efforts around the 5 minute mark always impresses me.Aggrandizement is debatably my favorite Deluge Grander track. I love the transition around 8:10 and later 10:57 or so. And the album rounds things off with the title track which brings the experience to a beautiful conclusion that's sweet but once again, grandiose. There's a lot of imagination behind this album that doesn't feel samey or out of place. It's also nice to be able to walk into a room and immediately know who's playing and with every single Deluge Grander album I'm able to do so. Not always in a good way but with The Form of the Good it's in the best of ways.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — The gift that keeps on giving, time after time. Just when you think the well is drying up, the spouting prog fountains spurt out another magnificent discovery. This has been a tradition for more than half a century and fits well within the Italian appreciation for dramatics in art , design, food and culture. This is their second offering after the 2024 debut "Pindaric Flights", which continues to feature composer, lead vocalist and keyboardist Marco Pantozzi. On that first album, he sung in English and now presumably by 'osmosis' , he has switched to his native language, always a great idea when dealing with RPI. In addition, he has brought in a few storied names to help out , namely the incredible keyboardist Vincenzo Ricca of the celebrated The Rome Pro(g)ject (a Prog Rogue favourite) and the talented Gigi Cavalli Cocchi on the drumkit (as well as the artwork), having made a name for himself with a slew of Italian prog bands such as Moongarden, Acqua Fragile, Ambigram Aerostation, Alex Carpani Band, Mangala Vallis, as well as few other collaborations. Ten nicely compact tunes, perfectly executed and each having both an original hue and a specific atmosphere, naturally drenched in massive dollops of emotional excitement. An entire panorama of moods is offered, seemingly with effortless musicianship, a painstakingly crafted album, that constantly confounds expectations yet always feeling in harmony with what came before and what one may be expecting next. The sonic curtains are drawn on the instrumental "Behind the Window", an instant plunge into a technical prowess that exudes confidence and inspiration. Ricca's keyboard dexterity should not come as any surprise; his playing is magnificence incarnate. Cocchi keeps the percussive line, Nicolo Magistrali on the bass and Gianmarco Mento on the guitars add all the necessary stringed adornments one could wish for. Emphatic and grandiose on the outside, fragile and suave beyond the frame. A stupendous first step. The path is now illuminated enough to focus on the melancholia-drenched "Mare Tranquillitatis", Marco's voice slicing through the mist of inner time and outer space, the Mento guitar stinging in the blue-hued distance, a floating expedition that seemingly has no dark side ?Elegant simplicity on the gentle lullaby, blanketed by a melody that makes one wander further than the daily routine, "Partire" has and added quality that it transcends categorization, easily playable on any radio or playlist without causing any grievance. Dreamy sonorities on the electro-acoustic psychedelia presented on "Fantasie Pindariche" , a Claudia Ursino vocal duet with Marco that shudders with goosebumps and arching voice elevations that intertwine into an upward vortex that is to die for. The twirling guitar pyrotechnics enhance the satisfaction. The flaming romanticism is consolidated on the more conventional piece "Arrendersi Mai" that suddenly, out of the blue sky, has Italian prog rapping ? Is there such a beast? The intense piece suggests a link to operetta with a prog sauce, a cry to never surrender or give in to anyone or anything. Feisty. The tragedy comes through on the segue "L'Emporio dell'Inganno" (the emporium of deceit or the name of the band, if you will), a very Italian slice of theatrical sophistication that concludes the section perfectly. The highlight track is the wholly unexpected beauty of "Norwegian Fjord", a glittering instrumental jewel that forces the listener to immediately close their eyes and ingest the sounds that engulf the spirit. Ricca proving once and for all, that the piano can be the most splendored instrument, all passionate restraint and intense resonation. A solo spotlight for the ages.Speaking of piano, Joe Chiericati takes over the ivories on the fluent "Panta Rei", an ebb and flow with a rousing guitar-organ driven interjection, keeping the juices bubbly. From this point on, the upcoming stylistics will slightly curve into a more personal and reflective mindset, especially evident as the singing becomes more sedate and meaningful. "La Risposta a Tutto" showcases some of the finest quality vocal presentations that flood this entire recording , within the confines of amazing melodic backbone. The closing track shines brightly with a sunshiny fragility, garnished with delightful female vocals, enchanted flute and a leisurely pace. "Raccontami di Te" tells one all they need to know. Frankly, each and every track is a winner, a truly remarkable foray that bodes well for the future. Nothing is ever predictable or even overblown with unnecessary dross, an Italian river of constant change. Because this group yearns for an ongoing career and audience, this is an artist that will deserve to be followed. 4.5 deceit depots

items.body: Review by Molloy — Once I said many of melodies created by this talented team can act as a perfect soundtrack to amovie. I would say this album is a new stage in the artistic development of Ivan and his peersbecause any theme in this work IS a movie with real plot twists, suspense moments, climaxes, andendings, happy or not. All the themes are inventive, expressive, and I would highly visual. Usingonly the power of the sound Ivan literally paints a dynamic series of pictures (always very personaland subjective of course) like in cartoons. By its free flow of an artist's thought and impetuousand continuous change of surrealistic images this collection looks like a third season of ShiveringTruth by Vernon Chapman expressed in the language of music, though more diverse in its moods andgenres. Every theme is like a story. It can a fairy tale like I need you to help, or a ballad likeNarrow in the Road, or sometimes even a detailed documentary, though full of cry and tragedy, likeKramatorsk. And every one is a real gem and masterpiece. A great deal of effort is felt in everycomponent of this work. One of the best if not the best album of Ivan and his team. Mycongratulations!

items.body: Review by Molloy — The wind bloweth where it listeth" may be the best epigraph to the entire works by Ivan Rozmainsky.Yet paradoxically this album combines a free flight of the musical thought in every individualpiece, typical for this artist, with an elaborate and strict design of the collection as a whole. Itis why some compositions require to be listened several times for better understanding them in thecontext of the whole album. Yet although each element of the entire construction plays its roleperfectly, some of them do it especially well. A real gem of the album is the opening piece, FollowAfter Meekness, with its mysterious sound and nervous pace. To continue this journey we travel upDifferent Sides of Ascension, another masterpiece, truly inventive in depicting the stages of thehuman spirit's adventure, to justify its title. A warm, mundane (in a good sense of this word) andvery human sound of Hard-Won Humility (may be my favorite peace of the whole album) can adorn anyprog rock collection. Definitely an amazing work by Ivan and his team. Hopefully, we will keep onenjoying the different sides of ascension of these great artists to new peaks of the musicalperfection.

items.body: Review by Stoneburner — Asceta, the Chilean band led by Rodrigo Maccioni, released their 2026 album, The Fool Leading the Blind. The band's music is often classified as chamber rock or RIO, but labels hardly do it justice. This is an extraordinary album, a pleasure to hear from start to finish, filled with meticulously crafted avant-garde music.The influences are unmistakable I can hear echoes of Zappa, Zorn, and King Crimson, as well as Schnittke and Varèse. Yet, in this carefully orchestrated musical orgy, everything is so thoughtfully structured that those influences gradually fade away, leaving only Asceta's own distinctive voice.With just five compositions, the album completely envelops the listener, revealing new details and becoming more fascinating with every spin. It is unlike anything I've heard in 2026, a truly original and rewarding listening experience.And that is the album's greatest achievement: rather than sounding derivative, it absorbs its inspirations and transforms them into something unique.

items.body: In his latest Secret History of Film Music column, Philip Brophy analyses Jonny Greenwood's score for Paul Thomas Anderson's One Battle After Another (2025) It’s hard to put your finger on how Jonny Greenwood’s commissioned score operates in Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another (2025). Not because the music is vague, indistinct or haphazard, but because it’s so deeply embedded in the story’s tight dramaturgy. It never feels like it’s accompanying anything. The music doesn’t come from the movie: it resides within the movie. This is the purported theoretical role of film music – to be wedded to everything on screen – but such audiovisual consummation is mostly over-rationalised while making grand claims of emotional evocation. Greenwood’s score pushes against such forced marriage, and his score is a series of miniatures stretched beyond any modest length, temporally extended through hesitancy and separation. Notes more than chords; points more than gestures. One Battle After Another boasts an impressive ensemble cast, and the film continues Anderson’s focus on how actors enable a film to reveal its energies – something he learnt from Orson Welles’s adoption of a stock company. This entails theatre mechanisms, especially in pre-production, through chemistry reads, group dynamics and character interplay. Sean Penn likened Anderson’s method to “hearing the music of [his] character”, when reflecting on how the director wrote the Colonel Lockjaw character. One Battle After Another is a prime example of a film in which a director functions like a conductor, and actors transform themselves into sensing instruments. This accounts for Greenwood’s role in the film’s group-oriented staging. He provides Anderson a range of possibilities within which the director finds shape, direction and purpose. It’s a type of displaced compositional strategy; a bi-fluxional method, where the composer is imagining what might be the musical environment in the director’s mind from which he could then construct a scene. Audited in isolation, the score feels like a mirage of a traditional recital: a largish ensemble, accentuated violin lines, studied percussive patterns, and dexterous piano playing, all ebbing and flowing with impressive dynamic range. While cinema fetishises ‘orchestrality’ as a cheap sign of performative quality, Greenwood’s orchestration is activated by textural exploration – not in expanded or improvisational form, but as semiotic reference. Orchestral grandeur is here demoted to being entrained by the prosaic machinations of human drama and its endless cycle of fight-or-flight pulsation. The film’s early theme “One Battle After Another” is tentatively built from a piano’s single note modulating through thrummed chords. Its cautious tone is decimated by a loud and sudden burst of a full string section shadowing the piano chords. This irrational dynamic matches the lo-fi amateur stealth of the terrorist group French 45, as we watch Perfidia (Teyana Taylor) and Pat (Leonardo DiCaprio) prepping for their attack on a border detention camp. Yet the music is bereft of dangerous heroics and full of regret, as if it knows what will be the consequences of Perfidia and Pat’s actions. I’m reminded of how Charles Ives’s The Unanswered Question is a deep well of conflicting emotions through its time-lagged and harmonically-displaced logic, via its wind instruments whose hive mind seems to be sited in another dimension. Greenwood’s theme here similarly finishes with trembling notes like waves lapping at an uncertain shoreline. Like most of the cues throughout One Battle After Another, the opening theme runs across multiple scenes and returns twice more. The result is a score shaped through triaxial statements, with themes versioned up to three times, each sounded to reveal something more about the characters’ pressures. (The cues’ official titles only match one of their accompanying scenes.) Metallic cymbal tones created by the violins’ stacked harmonics (“Baktan Cross 1”) sizzle as the terrorist crew creep toward a border crossing station. An orchestral drone swells, combined with passing trucks, dragged chainlink gates and night crickets. In this soundworld, Perfidia first encounters Colonel Lockjaw (Penn). The music seems to sonify their charged environment and the brooding fog of unleashed adrenaline germane to dangerous pursuits. But the music syncs to something more disturbing: Perfidia lectures Lockjaw (“Free borders! Free choice! And free from fear!”) while forcing his sexual arousal, mind-fucking his racist supremacist core while getting hot herself. Later, when Lockjaw discovers that Perfidia has Pat as her boyfriend, a maddening tick-tocking theme is activated (“French 75”). Rendered by a slightly prepared piano tapping a woodpecker waltz with woodblocks simulating a metronome, the notes idly dance up the keys and down again. Infantile, tentative, nervously staccato, it simulates a child’s hand – disturbingly so, as the theme trails Lockjaw’s shark eyes and craggy mask as he closes in on Perfidia, eventually encountering her in the toilet as she is wiring a bank with explosives. The theme will be repeated again, intensifying the ‘pleasure trauma’ of Lockjaw’s psychosexual rage and Perfidia’s orgone accumulation. The menacingly erotic image of a heavily pregnant Perfidia firing a machine gun, crowning her exposed belly with its magazine and screaming in joy, is accompanied by gunfire that obliterates the soundtrack. It is followed by a gentle baroque theme played on classical guitar (“For Willa”) which plays over a montage of Perfidia and Pat’s decaying relationship, culminating in her walking out on Pat and their newborn child, Charlene. The guitar feels church-like, but Perfidia is more Tony Montana than Lady Madonna, spitting at Pat, “This is a new consciousness.” Tied to a hospital bed after being captured following a botched bank robbery, she faces Lockjaw dangling the prospect of eluding jail time if she rats on members of the French 75. The funereal tonality of “Trust Device” commences, played by ondes Martenot and high strings as she confronts her own will to survive at the expense of her family. The theme continues as Pat prepares to go completely underground with his baby daughter. Both themes are instigated by Perfidia; both perform as a sorrowful ‘human Sanctus’ – Perfidia’s “new consciousness” – as her liberating actions tragically impact others. But as Pat departs, the music transforms into a warm lilt with light bossa rhythms tapped underneath, “Baby Charlene”. Distant hope is implied. It carries over Perfidia being relocated to a witness protection home, implying even hope for her, and symbolically tying mother and daughter together despite their impossible union. Greenwood’s cues are not simply emotive. Rather, they are dynamically interrelational, in accordance with the overall group interplay of the ensemble and their characters. Individuals are less activating than their relationships. This characterises how his cues don’t evolve as much as they shed their skin. They often devolve through repelled transitions, as if they can’t bear their own emotional weight. “Baby Charlene” is skinned to reveal a rising chorale of strings as Lockjaw discovers that Perfidia has escaped. Close in on his weathered scowl as he reads her sarcastic note, “This pussy won’t pop for you.” This brings us to the halfway mark of One Battle After Another. The aforementioned ‘triaxial’ distribution of cues multiple times in different scenes continues, deepening psychic drive and widening emotional composure in all the characters. Notably, the second half of the film shuttles 16 years later to the present, causing the music to resonate with the past. The opening piano theme returns in a deconstructed form as “Perfidia Beverly Hills” when Lockjaw has been accepted into the white supremacist Christmas Adventurers Club. A piano ostinato lumbers while strings rise and twist like a Bartók-ian ecosystem of fungal harmonic growth. Siren-like portamento ascents aerate the strings’ harmonic progression, pushing them upwards from an orchestral floor to an ecstatic canopy of upper register climes. It’s neither ironic nor cynical; it feels despairing of how nihilistic the control and display of power can be. Bob receives a phone call as Plan Snap Crackle Pop springs into action, but Bob is high and can’t recall the codes and prepared rendezvous points (“I Need The Greeting Code”). Herrmannesque strings wind around him like a stoner smoke haze – just like the tear gas that will engulf him as he crawls through his escape tunnel. Once he surfaces in the woods, a thumping piano cue starts, “Ocean Waves (Pt 1)”. It’s a very long cue, ratcheting the temporal shrinkage of all Bob must undertake in order to elude Lockjaw’s pursuit and reunite with Willa. Itching piano notes percolate as Bob desperately tries to remember the secret codes. They continue over the extended scene of Bob meeting karate sensei Sergio (Benicio del Toro) who will be aiding his flight. The scene flits throughout the labyrinth of Sergio’s Sanctuary City multi-floored home as he prepares his multitude of refugees to escape while Bob desperately tries to remember those passwords on his charging cell phone. As an ICE team breaks into the building, toms tap 3/4 time atop the piano pecking and occasional orchestral jitters. It’s like the orchestra is being told by the piano to not play. The instrumentation evokes Charles Ives reinterpreting Japanese gagaku court music, here shorn of any exoticist seduction and rendered fretful and agitated. Tackling Anderson’s commissioned scores requires substantial analysis. For now, this essay cannot venture further with One Battle After Another. Elsewhere I’ve written overly long breakdowns of Jon Brion’s score for Magnolia (1999) and Greenwood’s score for Inherent Vice (2015). However, next month’s essay will consider two uncredited Brion tracks (not on the Nonesuch release) used at formative and conclusive moments in One Battle After Another, and unravel Brion’s legacy in Anderson’s approach to commissioning music. Wire subscribers can read Philip Brophy’s original Secret History of Film Music columns from the 1990s online in the digital archive. Previous instalments of this column published on The Wire website can be found here.

items.body: Don’t wanna talk about it Just wanna scream about it Sun Spoiler locked himself in a room on the Fourth of July, which is either the beginning of a personal reckoning or the opening scene of a low-budget horror film where the fireworks outside are celebrating everybody except the poor bastard holding the guitar. Out of that sealed chamber came Reek, a 101-second nervous breakdown with a hook sharp enough to puncture the glowing rectangle that ruined his week. “Every line in Reek is the truth.” Andreas Emmanuel, the Greek-American guitarist behind the Los Angeles project, takes three weeks of romantic acceleration, digital humiliation, sexual memory, and spectacular self-disgust and crams them into a song that moves with the reckless efficiency of somebody fleeing a burning apartment while still checking whether she viewed his story. Lovebombing, breadcrumbing, ghosting: modern romance now arrives with the vocabulary of psychological warfare and the customer-service experience of a budget airline. The arrangement is lean, rude, and ridiculously catchy. Guitar, bass, drums, synths, cello, upright bass, baglama, otamatone—Emmanuel can apparently play everything except emotionally unavailable, though “Reek” suggests he has recently received a brutal lesson from somebody else. None of those instruments get to grandstand. They pile into the getaway car, slam the doors, and race through a jagged little collision of garage rock, post-punk, mutant pop, and the kind of college-radio lunacy that once made the mid-’90s feel dangerous after midnight. There is some Iggy Pop in the exposed nerve, some Pixies in the compact violence, and enough Garden-style mischief to keep the misery from turning into a wet blanket. The Bauhaus-meets-LMFAO comparison sounds deranged until the song starts grinding forward with funeral-club cheek, at which point it becomes alarmingly reasonable. You can picture a goth basement full of people dancing while one guy near the speaker mouths every word with the ruined concentration of a man composing a curse he promised never to cast. Emmanuel has worked as a session guitarist with Yves Tumor, Cullen Omori, Fatal Jamz, Georgi, and others, yet “Reek” feels proudly unbeholden to professional polish. Its appeal lies in compression: the romance, the flowers, the vanished woman, the preserved strand of hair, the party he cannot face, the phone he wants to destroy, all rushing past before dignity can intervene. At 1:41, Reek contains zero filler because heartbreak has already wasted enough of his time. It is funny, sick, frantic, intimate, and catchy as hell…the sound of a man turning emotional roadkill into a radio hit before the smell leaves the room. For once, oversharing becomes quality control: every ugly detail earns its place, every joke lands beside a bruise, and the song exits before anyone can offer advice, closure, or a wellness podcast. The video releases Emmanuel among crumbling stone chambers and iron cages, where he claws at the bars, writhes against the walls, and crowds the handheld camera with a succession of aggrieved close-ups. Hard sunlight, jump cuts, and shots of him thrashing on an angular guitar turn the ruins into a feral little theater for romantic humiliation. items.body: Before you fell I knew your name Before the dusk devoured day Yet still you cast your stone And still you are alone For more than a decade, NITE have been refining a strain of dark electronic pop that treats emotional excess with composure. The Texas group, led by twin brothers Myles and Kyle Mendes with drummer Phil Helms, have moved through several album cycles since forming in 2013, gathering an audience only recently as clips of their music began circulating across social media. That unlikely acceleration has introduced younger listeners to a vocabulary drawn from synthpop, post-punk, and darkwave, while sold-out appearances in the United States and Europe have given the band’s long development a sudden public scale. Cries for Help makes clear why the response has gathered force. Its arrangement is spacious, severe, and balanced, with synths that seem to hang at odd angles around the vocal rather than settling into a familiar wash. Myles Mendes sings with a graceful, wounded control that recalls the emotional precision of Talk Talk and Bronski Beat, the cool architecture of The Human League, and the polished ache of Pet Shop Boys. NITE have developed a voice that feels their own: formal, romantic, and alert to the humiliations that accompany love when care hardens into obligation. The song concerns the point at which compassion reaches exhaustion. Every plea becomes part of another cycle of dependency, frustration, and collapse, until devotion begins to resemble permission. Its doomed central figure has been heard, recognised, and offered what they claimed to need, yet continues breaking apart while striking at those nearby. The emotional pressure comes from the recognition that love cannot repair a void another person will not face. Stepping away becomes an act of mercy, although the decision carries the cold knowledge that the fall may already be irreversible. That tension is intensified by the strange atmosphere surrounding the melody. Synth tones drift in with an almost architectural unease, leaving pockets of air around the drums and bass, while the vocal rises through the mix with an elegance that makes the lyric’s despair feel even more exposed. Grandeur can sharpen intimacy when every element has room to breathe. Their self-directed black-and-white video extends the song’s emotional logic through the theme of separation. The band performs in the same interior, yet each member occupies a private zone: divided by mirrors, caught on a telephone, or framed alone while others remain close by. Nobody fully connects, and the room begins to resemble a set of adjacent cells. Shot with the severe beauty of an early music-video melodrama, the film turns distance into choreography. Watch the video for Cries for Help below: Cries for Help finds NITE converting emotional fatigue into poised, exacting pop, with every measured gesture carrying the weight of a relationship nearing its final limit. Listen to Cries for Help below and order the single here. NITE by Nite NITE’s 2026 touring schedule takes the band across North America and Europe, beginning with Calgary’s Terminus Festival before an August run through the South, East Coast, and Midwest with Echos. UK and Czech dates follow, leading into a West Coast co-headlining tour with Julien-K from late September through early October. The itinerary closes with Texas appearances alongside Dead on a Sunday and Panic Priest. items.album: Italian Outfit Ponte del Diavolo Discusses Their Signature Post-Punk Doom

items.body: Turin has historically provided heavy music characterized by a sense of architecture, drama, and subterranean grandeur, while Ponte del Diavolo has constructed its own imposing structure using those same elements. Formed during the winter of 2020 through a jam involving members of Feralia, Inchiuvatu, Abjura, and Askesis, the group developed a concentrated fusion of doom, black metal, post-punk, and wave that they describe as “blackened post-punk.” Its force comes from an arrangement as unusual as it is imposing: two bass guitars form the low, dense foundation, while Nerium’s guitar cuts across the rhythm with sharp economy and Segale Cornuta’s drums keep the music tense, physical, and unpredictable. At the center stands vocalist Erba del Diavolo, whose wave-informed delivery gives the band’s esoteric language its commanding presence. Alongside bassists Krhura Abro and Kratom, she helps turn the group’s old-school metal roots toward colder, stranger terrain, where doom’s mass meets post-punk’s disciplined motion and black metal’s feral edge. The contrast between these elements produces music that feels ceremonial without losing momentum, vast without surrendering detail. After issuing three EPs, Ponte del Diavolo signed with Season of Mist and released their debut album, Fire Blades from the Tomb. Two years of touring followed, including appearances at major European festivals such as Roadburn and Inferno, where the band’s uncommon instrumentation and theatrical intensity found a wider audience. They now return with De Venom Natura, an album that pushes their established language into more expansive and intricate forms. The record sharpens the interplay between voice, bass, guitar, and drums while deepening the ominous atmosphere that has defined the group from the beginning. Ponte del Diavolo enter this next chapter with greater control, broader reach, and a clear sense of their singular place between metal’s ancient foundations and post-punk’s austere pulse in the European underground and far beyond. Ponte del Diavolo spoke with Post-Punk.com about the album: Ponte Del Diavolo draws from doom and black metal as well as post-punk, deathrock, and gothic rock. Which post-punk artists first made a lasting impression on each of you, and what elements of their work eventually entered the band’s music? KRATOM: The first artists that come to my mind are Bauhaus, early Christian Death, Virgin Prunes, Burning Image, and Killing Joke. The most obvious thing they brought to our music is, of course, the pulsating, driving bass lines, but also the melodies that are creepy, unsettling, and romantic at the same time. Most of the recordings by the artists I mentioned are also raw in terms of sound quality, which is something I find very appealing too. You can feel a visceral passion, in a similar fashion to old black metal recordings. Kratom, the band’s dual-bass configuration gives Ponte Del Diavolo an unusual foundation. How do the two bass parts divide their roles, and how has post-punk’s emphasis on the bass guitar shaped your approach to rhythm, melody, and atmosphere? KRATOM: Having two basses in the mix is both a big challenge and a big creative outlet. As you said, the post-punk genre is famous for having the bass as the driving force of the compositions, and this is in stark contrast with the black metal approach, where the bass is most of the time completely buried in the background or almost non-existent. It was certainly a bold move on our part to double down and mix these very different approaches with an additional bass, but I have to say we really love the end result. That being said, managing two basses in the mix is no easy task, and with each record we try to improve the chemistry between them and get a better overall blend. Erba, gothic rock frequently treats the voice as both a storytelling instrument and a physical presence. Which vocalists or performers helped shape your delivery, and how do you adapt that theatrical tradition to Ponte Del Diavolo’s own identity? Erba: That’s a tough question for me, mostly because it’s never a deliberate choice. Instead, it’s the result of a lifelong alchemy, a mix of every concert I’ve ever witnessed, the bands I’ve listened to until exhaustion, and the gothic musical aesthetic, which is simply what resonates most naturally within me. I’m certain that the towering, luciferian presence of Diamanda Galás, the elegant, punk vampire prince movements of Peter Murphy, and the melancholic sweetness of Robert Smith have all shaped me. So too have the liminality of silent cinema (Cinema Strange embody this perfectly), the esoteric and magical depth of The Mission and Fields of the Nephilim, the ethereal spirit of Dead Can Dance, the unsettling sensuality of Rozz Williams, and the ritualistic commanding presence of Siouxsie. All of these elements have filled my own personal Pandora’s box, and it is a box I gladly empty in front of everyone, every time I step onto the stage. Il Veleno della Natura, from Ponte del Diavolo’s latest album, De Venom Natura, brings the band’s melodic post-punk and gothic-rock qualities particularly close to the surface. Could you take us through how the song developed, including its basslines, guitar melody, vocals, and lyrics? What does “the poison of nature” signify within the song, and how did the video’s alchemical laboratory setting extend those ideas? KRATOM: The song particularly stands out in terms of the dual basslines accompanying the groovy verses. The main bass riff comes from Abro (the other bassist), who is a big fan of The Cure, and I think you can hear the influence in the melody. I also think the synths (played by our dear friend Lucynine) play a major role in giving the song its “electro-wave”, eerie feel. Erba: The poison of nature’ speaks of transformation of nature’s movement as a perpetual cycle of life, death, and rebirth. That poison can carry various meanings, depending entirely on the listener. I don’t really like to dissect or over-explain my lyrics because it strips away the poetry; it almost robs the audience of their right to give the song their own personal meaning. I believe art should be exactly like that: taking shape and living a different life inside whoever experiences it. Once it is fed to the public, it must have a life of its own. In any case, that poison acts differently depending on the eyes of the beholder, or how it manifests in the lives of those who endure it, whether actively or passively. It is a fermenting agent that can either become your personal creative spark or the very cause of your death. And we aren’t necessarily talking about drugs here, in this case, I might be referring to the magical power of humankind. Or perhaps not. Who knows? Lunga vita alla necrosi, another song from De Venom Natura, takes the album’s post-punk current into heavier territory more closely aligned with deathrock. What inspired the song’s central rhythm and escalating intensity? Please also discuss the meaning of its title and lyrics, and how the video’s changing procession of occult and psychedelic images reflects the music. Erba: Lunga Vita alla Necrosi is the flip side of the coin to Demone, a track from our previous album Fire Blades From The Tomb. It represents what happens to the human soul when, paralyzed by the fear of change or the desperate need to cling to a fragile illusion of security, one fails to follow their own inspiration, their true nature, their inner demon. As for the video? It’s a relentless procession of decay and putrefaction. It mirrors the state of a soul that refuses to be honest with itself. KRATOM: You’re right, this is the song on De Venom Natura that definitely has the most deathrock vibes. It’s an upbeat song, but dark and heavy as well. I channeled my punk influences for the main bassline, and when Nerium added his black metal guitar riff on top of that, it really clicked for us. Covenant, from Ponte del Diavolo’s 2024 debut album, Fire Blades from the Tomb, moves at a slower, more ominous pace, allowing tension to accumulate gradually. How did you construct that sense of weight and expectation? What kind of covenant is invoked in the lyrics, and why did you choose Turin’s ancient, monastery-like monuments and a cemetery as settings for the video? Erba: We didn’t want any religious undertones. In fact, I think I can speak for the whole band when I say that religions disgust us, every single one of them. What we actually wanted was to use the ancient monuments of the city we grew up in. To us, they don’t feel religious; they feel imposing, ancient, weathered by time, filthy, and deathly. And because of that, they are incredibly beautiful, just like the cemetery where the entire second half of the video was filmed. As for Covenant, it represents a gathering of natural elements. While I was writing the lyrics, I fantasized about them organizing themselves to break free and sweep humanity away completely. Your cover of Bauhaus’s In the Flat Field appears on De Venom Natura. Why did you choose this particular song, and what does it mean to you personally? Your interpretation feels icier and more theatrical than the original. How did you decide which recognizable features to preserve and which elements to reshape in Ponte del Diavolo’s image? Erba: Choosing In the Flat Field came from pure love for Bauhaus; I’ve always dreamed of singing one of their tracks, though I’m deeply aware of the sheer greatness of the artists I’m covering. The song’s core resonates with me on a deeply personal level. I suffer terribly from boredom, and I completely reject the suffocating routine of everyday life; that sense of existential frustration is practically a reflection of my own personality. When it came to the music, we didn’t overthink it. The truth is, when we play together, that heavy theatrical sound is just what comes out of us completely naturally. It’s still Bauhaus, but dragged through our own darkness. Looking across these four recordings—Covenant from Fire Blades from the Tomb, followed by Il Veleno della Natura, Lunga vita alla necrosi, and your cover of In the Flat Field from De Venom Natura—how has Ponte del Diavolo’s relationship with post-punk changed between the two albums? Has that influence become more pronounced, or have you found new ways of integrating it with the band’s heavier foundations? KRATOM: I would say both. The influences were always there, but throughout these years of live shows and records we have grown as musicians and as a band, and we have become more aware and conscious of our sound, which we have decided to label “blackened post-punk”. It’s a term that could really mean everything and nothing, but I feel it’s the most correct way to define our music. We have definitely learned how to integrate different elements better, and as a band we find it very appealing to push our sonic boundaries. We would love to expand them further in the future. Ponte del Diavolo’s latest album De Venom Natura is out now. Listen below, and order it here.
