items.excerpt: ■ 8回路モデルとは何か8回路モデルは、心理学者ティモシー・リアリー(Timothy Leary)が提唱し、その後リアリーと親交を深めたロバート・アントン・ウィルソンが発展させた意識・脳機能のモデルです。これはティモシー・リアリーによって心理学的哲学(psy-phi)として提示されたホリスティックなモデルで、人間の神経系の中で機能する8つの回路、あるいは他の著者が呼ぶところの8つのシステムや「脳」を仮定しています。各回路はそれぞれ独自のインプリント(刷り込み)と、現実についての主観的経験に対応するとされます。この理論はリアリーが著書『Neurologic』(1973年)や『Exo-Psychology』(1977年)で導入し、その後ロバート・アントン・ウィルソンが著書『Cosmic Trigger』(1977年)と『Prometheus Rising』(1983年)で発展させ、さらにAntero Alliが著書『Angel Tech』(1985年)や『The Eight-Circuit Brain』(2009年)で「8つの期間(回路)」があると論じました。1960年代後半から1970年
items.body: ■ 8回路モデルとは何か8回路モデルは、心理学者ティモシー・リアリー(Timothy Leary)が提唱し、その後リアリーと親交を深めたロバート・アントン・ウィルソンが発展させた意識・脳機能のモデルです。これはティモシー・リアリーによって心理学的哲学(psy-phi)として提示されたホリスティックなモデルで、人間の神経系の中で機能する8つの回路、あるいは他の著者が呼ぶところの8つのシステムや「脳」を仮定しています。各回路はそれぞれ独自のインプリント(刷り込み)と、現実についての主観的経験に対応するとされます。この理論はリアリーが著書『Neurologic』(1973年)や『Exo-Psychology』(1977年)で導入し、その後ロバート・アントン・ウィルソンが著書『Cosmic Trigger』(1977年)と『Prometheus Rising』(1983年)で発展させ、さらにAntero Alliが著書『Angel Tech』(1985年)や『The Eight-Circuit Brain』(2009年)で「8つの期間(回路)」があると論じました。1960年代後半から1970年代初頭にかけて、リアリーは作家ブライアン・バリット(Brian Barritt)との共同作業の中で8回路モデルの原型を形成していきました。エッセイ「The Seven Tongues of God」では人間の脳には7つの回路があり7段階の意識レベルを生むと主張し、これは獄中で執筆した1973年の論文集『Neurologic』では7回路説になりました。8回路説が完全な形で定式化されたのは、リアリーの『Exo-Psychology』とウィルソンの『Cosmic Trigger』が発表された1977年のことです。■ 全体構造:地球回路と地球外回路このモデルの8つの回路のうち、最初の4回路は地球上の生活と人類種の生存に関わるものとされます。残りの4回路は「地球外的(post-terrestrial)」であり、いわゆる変性意識状態、悟り、神秘体験、サイケデリック体験、超能力といった、人類種の進化に関わるものとされています。 リアリーは最初の4つを「幼虫回路(larval circuits)」と呼び、地球社会で生存し機能するために必要なものとした一方、地球外回路は将来人類が宇宙移住への衝動に従って進化していく上で有用になると位置づけました。なお、リアリーはこの8回路を左脳・右脳の分化とも結びつけ、最初の4回路は左脳、残る4回路は右脳に宿るとする独自の脳機能局在論を展開しましたが、これは正統な神経心理学の裏付けを欠く飛躍だとされています。■ 8つの回路 各論(Wilson版の名称で)第1回路:口唇・生存回路(バイオサバイバル回路)乳児期に刷り込まれる、最初期の回路です。吸乳、栄養摂取、抱擁、身体的安全の確保に関わります。 無脊椎動物の進化の初期に出現したとされ、三位一体脳理論(triune brain theory)における爬虫類脳に対応し、哺乳類・爬虫類・魚類・霊長類・人間を通じて基本的に同じ働き方をするとされます。ウィルソンはこの回路をフロイトの心理性的発達理論における口唇期と同一視し、成人ではオピオイド系の薬物によって活性化されると論じました。第2回路:肛門・情動縄張り回路よちよち歩きの幼児期に刷り込まれ、縄張りの主張、感情による力の駆け引き、支配・服従の政治戦略に関わります。 ウィルソンはこれをフロイトの肛門期と同一視し、アルコールやバルビツール酸系、ベンゾジアゼピン系などの抑制系薬物によって活性化されるとしました。優位で攻撃的な行動はフリッツ・パールズの「トップドッグ」概念や交流分析における「I'm OK」のポジション、ニーチェの「主人道徳」に対応し、逆に従属的で協調的な行動は「アンダードッグ」「I'm not OK」「奴隷道徳」に対応するとされています。第3回路:喉頭・手指(時間束縛=意味論)回路人間の作った道具や記号体系によって刷り込まれ、環境の操作、発明、計算、予測、宇宙の「地図」の構築に関わります。 ウィルソンは一般意味論(ゼネラル・セマンティクス)に強く影響を受けており、この回路を「時間束縛(タイム・バインディング)回路」として論じ、人類の知識やノウハウが世代を超えて蓄積されていく機能を担うとしました。覚醒剤やコカインなど刺激系薬物によって活性化されるとされます。第4回路:社会性・性(道徳)回路初めてのオーガズムを伴う性経験や部族の「道徳」によって刷り込まれ、性的快楽、地域ごとの「道徳的/不道徳」の定義、生殖、子育てに関わります。 ここに強く刷り込まれた人は性に執着するか、逆に極端に性否定的(あるいはその両方)になりやすいとされます。ここまでの第1〜4回路が、いわゆる「地球回路」です。第5回路:神経身体回路生理的あるいは化学的なヨガ(瞑想法や薬物体験)を通じた恍惚体験によって刷り込まれ、神経と身体のフィードバック、高揚感、身体的な再プログラミング(クリスチャン・サイエンスや信仰療法など)に関わります。第6回路:神経電気(メタプログラミング)回路高度なヨガによって刷り込まれ、それまでの全回路の再刷り込み・再プログラミング、知覚される「現実」の相対性、サイバネティックな意識に関わります。第7回路:神経遺伝子(モルフォゲネティック)回路同じく高度なヨガによって刷り込まれ、進化的意識(過去と未来)、DNA-RNA-脳のフィードバック、ユングの「集合的無意識」に関わります。 ウィルソンはこれを生物学者ルパート・シェルドレイクの形態形成理論(モルフォゲネシス理論)にちなんで「モルフォゲネティック回路」と呼びました。この回路が活性化した人は過去世、輪廻転生、不死などを語るようになるとされます。第8回路:神経原子(非局所的量子)回路ショックや臨死体験によって刷り込まれ、量子的意識、時空を超えた非局所的な気づき、いわゆる「サイ(PSI)」能力や「魔術」、そして「イルミネーション(悟り)」に関わります。 ESP、体外離脱体験、レビテーション、魔術など、いわゆる「超自然的」体験の大半がこの回路に結びつけられており、リアリーとウィルソンは量子論を援用してこれらの可能性を説明しようとしました。なお第6・7回路については、ウィルソンは『Prometheus Rising』において両者の順序を入れ替え、神経遺伝子回路を第6、メタプログラミング回路を第7としましたが、後の『Quantum Psychology』ではリアリー本来の順序に戻しています。この『Quantum Psychology』はE-プライム(be動詞を排した英語表記法)で書かれ、各章末に意識のエクササイズが収録されています。■ 主要な関連概念リアリティ・トンネル(reality tunnel)私たちは皆「リアリティ・トンネル」の中に存在している、というのがウィルソンの中心的な主張です。私たちは誰もが自分自身で構築した現実のバージョンの中に生きているにもかかわらず、それを完全な真実だと思い込んでいます。時に人間は突然の気づきによってそのトンネルの壁を目にし、そこから脱出することがあります。チャペル・ペリラス(Chapel Perilous)ウィルソンは、自分のリアリティ・トンネルが崩壊し始めたときに生じる心理状態を「チャペル・ペリラス」と表現しました。「チャペル・ペリラスは、おとぎ話の中の謎めいた存在のように、様々な形で現れうる。私の場合はコンピュータとして、リリーの場合は向精神薬として、ユングの場合はマンダラとして、クロウリーの場合は儀式として現れた。そこは、ジョークの意味を理解するか、狂気に陥るかのどちらかの場所である」。ここを抜けた者は「徹底したパラノイア」になるか、「アグノスティック(不可知論者)」になるとウィルソンは述べています。ゲリラ・オントロジー / モデル・アグノスティシズム「イルミナティ」「ディスコルディアニズム」「オペレーション・マインドファック」「リアリティ・トンネル」「モデル・アグノスティシズム」といった概念は、ロバート・アントン・ウィルソンただ一人によって現代文化の語彙の一部となりました。SMI²LE(空間移住・知能増進・寿命延長)1976年、ウィルソンは妻アーレンとともに設立した「人類の未来研究所」の活動の一環として、リアリーのSMI²LE哲学(Space Migration=宇宙移住、Intelligence Increase=知能増進、Life Extension=寿命延長)を実装するための「スターフライト・ネットワーク」を立ち上げ、あわせて8回路モデルの普及にも努めました。 この定式は、宇宙植民地(高軌道上のミニ地球=H.O.M.E.)への移住、人体の生物学的寿命の延長や死後の再生といったビジョンを表しており、1970〜80年代にリアリーとウィルソンが世界中を巡って情熱的に語り歩いたコンセプトでした。 6回路(メタプログラミング回路)が高度に活性化すれば、地球外知性体との高エネルギー通信すら可能になるともウィルソンらは述べています。■ Leary版とWilson版の違いウィルソンの1983年の著書『Prometheus Rising』は、リアリーの8回路モデルを詳細に解説したワークブックであり、また未製作に終わった1993年の脚本を書籍化した『Reality Is What You Can Get Away With』でもこのモデルが使われ解説されています。 リアリー自身の回路名(バイオサバイバル/情動縄張り/意味論/社会性・性/神経身体/神経電気/神経遺伝子/神経原子)に対し、ウィルソンはより分かりやすい呼称(口唇・肛門・喉頭手指・社会性性・神経身体・メタプログラミング・モルフォゲネティック・非局所的量子)を与えることで一般読者への浸透を図りました。■ 主要著作(原典)・ティモシー・リアリー『Neurologic』(1973)・ティモシー・リアリー『Exo-Psychology』(1977、のち『Info-Psychology』として改訂)・ロバート・アントン・ウィルソン『Cosmic Trigger I: The Final Secret of the Illuminati』(1977)・ロバート・アントン・ウィルソン『The Illuminati Papers』(1980、「8 Winner/Loser Scripts」収録)・ロバート・アントン・ウィルソン『Prometheus Rising』(1983、改訂1997)・アンテロ・アリ(Antero Alli)『Angel Tech』(1985)・ロバート・アントン・ウィルソン『Quantum Psychology』(1990)・ティモシー・リアリー&ロバート・アントン・ウィルソン『The Game of Life』(1993)・アンテロ・アリ『The Eight-Circuit Brain』(2009)・ロバート・アントン・ウィルソン『The Starseed Signals: A RAW Perspective on Timothy Leary』(2020、没後刊行)・Douglas S. Wingate、Rachel Turetzky(David Jay Brown協力)『8-Circuit Ascension: A Guide to Metaprogramming the Multidimensional Self』(2025)■ 学術的評価と批判このモデルは科学的信頼性を欠くとしてかねてより批判され、1970年にサイケデリック薬物が犯罪化されて以降、学界ではほぼ無視されてきましたが、サイケデリック医療への学術的・臨床的関心が再燃する中で、非日常的意識状態を扱う実践的枠組みとして近年再び注目を集めています。文化史家ジョン・ヒッグス(John Higgs)は、リアリーはサイケデリックから人類進化に関する思索へと軸足を移すことで学術的な評判を立て直そうとしたが、この「科学的信頼性を得ようとする試みは失敗する運命にあった。一つには彼が悪名高いティモシー・リアリーであり、その評判が常に彼につきまとったからであり、もう一つには、理論モデルを構築しながらそれが同時に複数の異なるものを表すと主張するのは、単純に良い科学とは言えないからである。この思考法は本質的にオカルト的・神秘主義的なものであり、決して学界から真剣に受け止められることはなかった」と述べています。より具体的な批判として、各回路に対応する神経解剖学的基盤(検証された神経相関)が示されていないこと、覚醒など基本的な意識状態に関わる他の神経構造が考慮されていないことが指摘されています。また、特定の薬物と特定の体験を結びつける主張にも疑問符がつけられており、たとえば第3回路(意味論回路、象徴的思考に関わる)はカフェインやコカインなど刺激剤によって活性化するとされますが、これらの薬物が本当に象徴的思考を促進するのかは疑わしいとされます。さらにリアリーは占星術やタロットを用いてこの理論を補強しようとしており、これが理論をより疑似科学的に見せる一因になっています。批判者は、リアリーの8回路モデルは根拠のない楽観主義に基づいており、その提示と擁護の過程でユートピア主義、疑似科学、エリート主義、精神的なナルシシズムに陥っていると指摘します。この理論は当時も現在も科学者によって真剣に検討・研究・議論されたことはありませんが、それでもサイケデリックが人々の態度や世界観に与えうる影響を示す事例としては省みる価値があるとされています。近年では学術的な再評価の動きもあり、Kasian、Turetzky、Wingateによる論文「Exploring the Eight-Circuit Model of Consciousness: A Pathway to Enhanced Mind-Body Health」(2024/2025年)が、この8回路モデルを扱った初の査読付き学術論文とされています。ただしWikipediaはこれを「信頼性の疑わしい周縁的情報源(unreliable fringe source)」の可能性があると注記しています。■ 文化的影響:カオスマジックからGrant Morrisonまで8回路モデルはカオスマジック(Chaos Magic)の分野でもかなり重要な位置を占めており、8つの回路はカオスのシンボルが持つ8本の光線と関連づけて理解されています。この概念はカオスマジック結社イルミネーツ・オブ・サナトス(Illuminates of Thanateros)の中心メンバーであるデイヴ・リー(Dave Lee)の著書『Chaotopia!』で詳述されました。リアリーとウィルソンはいずれも晩年この結社の会員でしたが、8回路のデザイン自体はこの組織の設立より以前から存在していました。アンテロ・アリは著書『Angel Tech』でモデルを実践・身体性・儀式的統合の方向へと展開させました。アリは8回路を優劣のある単純な梯子ではなく、8つの相互作用する知性の機能として描き直し、後の著作ではすべての回路が「価値において等しい」、それぞれが異なる度合いで潜在・統合されているに過ぎないと強調しています。作家グラント・モリソン(Grant Morrison、『The Invisibles』などで知られるコミック作家)は、2025年刊行の『8-Circuit Ascension』を「リアリーの8回路モデルへのこの見事なアップデートは、心理学、神経生物学、サイケデリック、マジック、メタプログラミング、人間の発達に関心を持つすべての人の本棚に置かれるべきだ」と評しています。このほか、ウィリアム・バロウズ、フィリップ・K・ディック、ラリー・ワコウスキー/リリー・ワコウスキー(『マトリックス』)などカウンターカルチャー・SF方面の作家たちにも、リアリティ・トンネルやメタプログラミングの概念を通じて間接的な影響を与えたとされ、超人間主義(トランスヒューマニズム)の源流の一つとしても言及されます。ウィルソンとリアリーは、後にトランスヒューマニストと呼ばれる思想家たちより数十年早く、実質的にトランスヒューマニズム的な思想を展開していたと評されています。■ 他の心理モデルとの比較8回路モデルは単体で存在するのではなく、しばしば以下のような既存モデルと対照されます。・エイブラハム・マズローの欲求段階説:phinnweb.orgの資料でも直接比較対象として挙げられており、いずれも「低次から高次へ」段階的に発達するという構造的な類似性が指摘されます。・カジミェシュ・ドンブロフスキの積極的分解理論(Positive Disintegration):同じくしばしば並べて論じられます。・ユングの集合的無意識:第7回路(神経遺伝子/モルフォゲネティック回路)と直接対応づけられます。・エリック・バーンの交流分析(Transactional Analysis)における「ライフポジション」:第1・第2回路の肯定的/否定的刷り込みが、それぞれ「I'm OK」「I'm not OK」のポジションと対応づけられています。・フリッツ・パールズのゲシュタルト療法における「トップドッグ/アンダードッグ」概念、ニーチェの「主人道徳/奴隷道徳」:第2回路の説明で援用されます。・ポール・マクリーンの三位一体脳理論(triune brain):第1・第2回路がそれぞれ爬虫類脳・哺乳類脳に対応づけられています。・ケン・ウィルバーのインテグラル理論/スパイラル・ダイナミクス:オンラインのディスカッションでは両者がしばしば比較され、どちらがより「実証的根拠」を持つかという論争が起きています。■ まとめ8回路モデルは、1960〜70年代のサイケデリック文化・サイバネティクス・オカルティズムが交錯する中から生まれた、いわば「対抗文化の意識地図」です。ティモシー・リアリーが骨格を作り、ロバート・アントン・ウィルソンが『Cosmic Trigger』『Prometheus Rising』『Quantum Psychology』を通じてより実践的・親しみやすい形に翻訳し、アンテロ・アリがさらに身体性と儀式的実践に落とし込みました。神経科学的な実証性という点では一貫して疑似科学だと批判され続けている一方、自己観察・信念体系の相対化・変性意識状態の言語化のための「詩的・実践的な地図」として、カオスマジックからサイケデリック・インテグレーション、近年の心身健康研究に至るまで、半世紀近くにわたって周縁的だが根強い影響力を持ち続けています。参考ソース(生きたリンク)Wikipedia「Eight-circuit items.body: 展覧会カタログ、アートやデザインにまつわる近刊書籍をアートスケープ編集部が紹介します。 建築は不純につくられる──中国・習近平時代の建築とモニュメント 著者：市川紘司 発行：岩波書店 発行日：2026年05月26日 サイズ：四六判、270ページ いまや東アジアの「建築家大国」となった中国。度肝を抜く奇抜なものから洗練されたデザインまで。実に多彩な現代建築の数々には矛盾や問題を抱えながらも急成長した中国社会の特性があらゆるかたちで埋め込まれている。『世界』人気連載「中国新建築文化論」に大幅に加筆修正してお届けする「中国現代建築入門」。図版多数。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   クリエイティブのための判断力──つくる人が考えるべきこと 著者：橋本俊行 発行：講談社 発行日：2026年06月25日 サイズ：四六判、190ページ AIでつくる手段が増えた今、問われるのは「何を選び、何を見送るか」。クリエイティブの現場で20年、判断を重ねてきた著者が、正解のない時代に自分の軸を育てるための考え方をまとめた一冊。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   芸術の発見──AI時代の生きる条件 著者：岡﨑乾二郎 発行：フィルムアート社 発行日：2026年06月26日 サイズ：A5判、216ページ いま発見される芸術、古代の問答術、よく生きることの意味。 AI終末論に対峙する「希望の書」、岡﨑乾二郎、最新の思考。 AIにつまずき、AIをつまずかせる──緊迫の応答、待望の書き下ろし。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］ 掌の美術論──触覚と想像力 著者：松井裕美 発行：勁草書房 発行日：2026年07月02日 サイズ：四六判、352ページ 遊びが手触りや感覚を頼りに新たなゲームや楽しさを創造し、ときに新しい認識や価値を開いていくように、触覚を軸にした鑑賞の方法を提示する。触覚に関わる美術史を整理したうえでフェミニズムや歴史・記憶と芸術作品の関係など、現代的な問題意識を織り込んだ作品解説を通し、触覚と想像力が拓く遊戯場としての美術史を紡ぎだす。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］ 建築の装飾──主体性と政治性のあいだ 著者：アントワーヌ・ピコン 訳者：千代章一郎 発行：鹿島出版会 発行日：2026年07月07日 サイズ：四六判、288ページ 装飾は、つねに政治的である。装飾の黎明から、モダニズムにおける拒絶、ポストモダニズムにおける失敗、そしてデジタル技術による復活まで。時代を横断して装飾の本質を問う、古くて新しい建築史。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   慶應義塾の槇文彦──建築とアーバニズム思想 編者：池田靖史 、小林博人、 大沼徹、渡部葉子 、新倉慎右 発行：慶應義塾大学出版会 発行日：2026年07月15日 サイズ：A5判、240ページ 槇文彦は、谷口吉郎設計の慶應義塾幼稚舎で学んだ幼少期を原風景として述懐している。後年は慶應の建築を多く手がけ、母校との絆を深めた。慶應義塾に残した槇の発言や関係者への取材、研究を通して世界的建築家の私的な交流をひもとく。 学び舎として、建築家として、学塾と歩んだ世界的巨匠の足跡 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   人工美学──生成AI・アート・ビジュアルメディア 著者：レフ・マノヴィッチ、エマニュエーレ・アリエッリ 監修：久保田晃弘 訳者：高崎拓哉 発行：BNN 発行日：2026年07月15日 サイズ：四六判、328ページ 本書は、美学、芸術哲学、芸術心理学、メディア論、デジタル文化研究、コンピュータ科学、そしてデジタルメディア実践の知見を横断しながら、生成AIが人間の感性と創作にもたらすインパクトを考察する。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］

items.body: 京都芸術センターと京都市中央青少年活動センターを舞台に、第30回 京都国際ダンスワークショップフェスティバル「京都の暑い夏」が開催されます。 30回目を迎える今回は、「Already Here」をテーマに、国内外で活躍する18名の講師により、ダンスを学ぶ人々が全国、そして世界から集う学びの場が創出されます。ワークショップやリサーチプログラムに加え、関西初となるジェローム・ベル作品の上演やトークなど、広く開かれた関連企画も行なわれます。 開催プログラム A：ダンスメソッド ダンサーとしての身体に必要なものは何か？身体の構造を理解すると共に、空間、時間、エネルギー、イメージ、そして創造性へと飛翔していく諸要素を学びます。また身体をケアしながらダンサーとしてより大胆に伸びやかに、自由に動けるよう身体の知恵を学びます。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 B：コンタクト＆インプロヴィゼーション 「身体と身体」の対話を具体的で物理的な法則に委ねて探究する「コンタクト・インプロヴィゼーション」。他者・空間・モノとの繋がり、対話を重視する多種多様な接触・コンタクトにまつわるクラスを設けます。自身と他者、世界とのコミュニケーション能力、Response-Ability（対応能力）を探究していきます。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 C：クリエイション＆リサーチ 国内外で活躍しているコレオグラファーが、固有のボキャブラリーおよび、創作のキーとなる考え／プロセスを参加者と共に探求します。参加者も自身の創造力を発揮しながら、それを掘り下げ、与えられるテーマに沿って作品創作の過程を体験します。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 D：インターディシプリナリー・プログラム “分野を横断した”という意味のインターディシプリナリー。このプログラムでは、多様な分野の専門的視点を通して、身体やダンスの捉え方を再発見・再認識するクラスです。ダンスの経験を問わず、幅広い視野を獲得し身体やダンスにアプローチしたい方にオススメです。 ■山極壽一 × 小倉笑 「山極壽一講座」座学編ワークショップ ■「山極壽一講座」実践編ワークショップ ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 E：京都芸術センター企画 ３つの「歩く」 いつ？どのように？どうして？どこを？誰と？ 「歩く」という行為、その一歩一歩が成立する背景には、どれほどの個性や表現の可能性が潜んでいるでしょうか。本企画では、それぞれの視点から「歩く」を探求する3人の実演家とともに「歩く」を実践し、再解釈することを試みます。並置される3つのアプローチを通して、「歩行」と「踊り」「表現」のあわいを辿ります。身体の感覚をひらき、新たな一歩に出会える2時間×３回のワークショップです。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 F：ビギナークラス コンテンポラリーダンスの多様性を満喫できるイントロダクション・クラス。国内外で活躍する講師による様々なスタイル、考え方、アプローチでダンスに触れることができるダンスの旅。通称、サラダボウルプログラム。五感六感総動員でトライ!。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 G：こどもと大人 子どもから大人まで、ダンスが初めての方も、大好きな方もウェルカム！このクラスでは、ダンス経験の違う参加者が、「踊る・動く・感じる・創る」ことを通して、ダンスの楽しさをのびのびと体験しながら学んでいきます。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 開催イベント ■ジェローム・ベル「ジェローム・ベル」上映 ■ショーイング ■大広間トークセッション ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 会期：2026/08/01（土）～2026/08/09（日） 会場：京都芸術センター（京都府京都市中京区室町通蛸薬師下る山伏山町546-2） 京都市中央青少年活動センター（京都市中京区東洞院通六角下ル御射山町262・3F） 問い合わせ先：京都国際ダンスワークショップフェスティバル事務局 一般社団法人ダンスアンドエンヴァイロメント TEL：070-6500-7242 E-mail：hotsummerinkyoto★gmail.com（★の部分を@に替えて送信してください） 主催：一般社団法人ダンスアンドエンヴァイロメント、京都芸術センター（公益財団法人京都市芸術文化協会） 公式サイト：https://hotsummer2026.studio.site

items.body: Who’s up for a hike? Rise and shine, ladies and gents! We’ve got quite the day ahead of us here on the J-Music Exchange/Rate, thanks in no small part to the particular album I have the pleasure of sharing with you all this month. If you’re one of our regulars, I’m sure you’re already geared up and ready to hit the trail with us. For those of you joining us for the very first time though, first off, welcome! Before we get underway, please give the following primer a quick read: The Exchange/Rate is a tandem album review series conducted every month by yours truly alongside my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al (from Omunibasu). Each month we decide on a specific theme with which our reviews would revolve around. We then pick out albums from our respective libraries which we think best coincides with that theme. We will then give the album we chose to the other person and vice versa (exchange), after which we then listen to and subsequently review the album we were given (rate). This project has not only allowed us to explore music beyond our libraries, but it provides an opportunity for us to see our favorite albums from a different point of view. It is our hope that this series is able to do the same for you and that you either find a new artist to try out and/or we offer you a fresh take on one of *your* favorite albums Al and I take turns deciding the theme for each month’s Exchange/Rate, and for July, the honors went back to him. His idea was for us to talk about albums that make you want to play/learn, an instrument. Not necessarily in the sense that they inspire you to start writing music yourself, but rather those moments where you hear a particular melody or performance and think, “Man, it’d be really cool to be able to play something like that.” Less about the songwriting, and more about the simple desire to pick up an instrument and give it a shot. To that end, I sent Al off to check out yubiori2 by yubiori, which you can read all about over at the Omunibasu Substack. In return, Al handed me Super Climbing Club’s self-titled debut album, Super Climbing Club, to share with you all today. So then… Let’s go hiking, shall we? ーー Formed in 2023 in Aichi Prefecture, Super Climbing Club (スーパー登山部) is a five-piece indie nature pop rock band built around a concept the concept of “mountains and music”. True to their name, the members don’t simply sing about mountaineering. They actually go out and climb mountains together, performing not only in live houses but even at mountain lodges sitting at elevations of around 3,000 meters. That same sense of adventure naturally carries over into the band’s music. Songwriter Oda Tomoyuki freely blends together folk, alternative rock, pop, jazz, and electronic influences to create songs that vividly evoke the feeling of being out in nature, while vocalist Hina’s crisp, airy singing gives everything an incredible sense of openness. ＜Ｓｕｐｅｒ Ｃｌｉｍｂｉｎｇ Ｃｌｕｂ (スーパー登山部)＞(＊Spotify link to the full album) CDJapan Affiliate Link(s):Super Climbing Club [Regular Edition] / Super Climbing Club ＜T ｒａｃｋｌｉｓｔ＞ ０１・Departure０２・Breathe０３・燕/tsubame０４・頂き/itadaki０５・いつかはね/itsukahane (Album Ver.)０６・hatoba (Album Ver.)０７・意志拾い/ishihiroi０８・ITAI０９・ハイライト/highlight１０・樹海/jukai feat. TENDRE１１・火花/hibana１２・木枯らし/kogarashi１３・スーパー銭湯もある/super sentou mo aru１４・風を辿る/kaze wo tadoru Ａｌ：Even though it’s probably in my best interest to go down this path, I am not much of an active or outdoorsy person. However, the idea of hiking, mountain climbing, camping, and exploring nature in general has always had an interesting connection to music, as it can often inspire people to listen to and/or create songs that exemplify the relaxing, calming atmospheres seen in those recreational activities. One well-known example that’ll come to most people’s minds (at least, to me and other Westerners who enjoy Japanese media) are the many anime soundtracks heard in shows that revolve around such pastimes, like Sora yori mo Tooi Basho, Non Non Biyori, and of course, Yuru Camp. They’re obvious mentions, I’ll admit, but I do genuinely give these shows (and the composers behind them) a lot of credit for introducing me to music that exert an upbeat, natural characteristic to them. While I’ve sought-out songs with a similar tone throughout my time as a Japanese music fan (e.g., Ohashi Trio, Kamishiraishi Mone, Hanaregumi), I don’t think you can find an artist that’s more dedicated to expressing outdoor recreation than a pop band full of actual & frequent mountain climbers. And just like the name of their band, and full-length album from this past June, suggests, Super Climbing Club truly does embody the sensations of taking in our natural environment. Even right from the beginning, “Departure” builds up to the dawn of a brand new day, while “Breathe” perfectly exudes a ‘bright-and-early’ energy that can put you in a confident mood in the morning. And I think why SCC is able to communicate this so well is definitely because of their instrumental abilities, where they express that lovely folksy tone through the soft flutes and keyboards, as well as the acoustic guitar melodies that easily remind me why the acogui is such a perfect and versatile instrument that’s worth playing and learning. But at the same time, it’s really neat to hear a group like them also branch out and try various styles that still fit well with the album’s overall theme. Whether it’s a gorgeous piano ballad that see vocalist Hina belt out a passionate performance, how the inclusion of an electric guitar adds some bite to certain songs (“Highlight”), or even that TAMTAM-esque chill reggae vibe heard on “Super Sento Mou Aru”… their whole background is certainly intriguing on its own, but for them to also be a bunch of talented musicians and singers that embrace their interests and convey that love through the art of music just makes them an even cooler band in my eyes. ＜Ｓｏｎｇｓ ｏｆ Ｉｎｔｅｒｅｓｔ＞ ０１・Departure、０２・BreatheIn as much as we tend to, if not always, talk about an album’s opening track here on the Exchange/Rate, I feel like it’s actually been a while since we’ve had a dedicated opener like Departure. Much like its namesake, and I have to imagine intentionally so, Departure feels like it’s trying to capture those quiet moments just before setting out on a long journey. It’s the crack of dawn; you’ve finished making your final preparations while everyone else is still asleep, and you’re standing at the beginning of what lies ahead. In an album spanning fourteen tracks, Super Climbing Club itself almost feels like its own mountain to climb, but I’ll come back to that thought a little later. As someone who almost always listens to an album from front to back, I personally love inclusions like this. Not because I think an introductory track is what makes or breaks an album, but because it encourages a continuous playthrough and gives the record a greater sense of continuity. That winds up paying off almost immediately as Departure seamlessly gives way to Breathe, the first full song on the album. If Departure is the moment before the journey begins, then Breathe feels like watching the sun slowly rise once you’re already on the road. You know those moments during a road trip when everyone in the car is still asleep, only for someone to wake everybody up because the sunrise outside is just too beautiful to miss? That’s exactly the image the song paints for me. It’s also here that we get our first proper taste of Super Climbing Club’s indie nature-pop sound, brought to life by Hina’s wonderfully crisp, airy vocals. Every time she sings, I can’t help but imagine a cool mountain breeze passing by. In fact, if I had to describe the band’s overall sound, I’d probably call it “Alps-like.” Not in the yodeling sense of the word, of course (lol), but in how vast and open everything feels. Hina’s voice creates an incredible sense of space that gives the music room to breathe, reminding me a lot of what I’ve written in the past about Kamishiraishi Mone’s singing. ０３・燕/tsubameI’ve since listened to Super Climbing Club a fair bit at the time of writing this review, and without fail, I always find myself coming back to Tsubame. To the point where, yes, I do think it’s ultimately my favorite track on the album. The song continues that outdoorsy atmosphere established by the first two tracks through Super Climbing Club’s organic folk-inspired guitar work, but presents it in a noticeably more pop-oriented fashion thanks to its subtle incorporation of synths and electronic beats. Those electronic touches are actually one of the defining characteristics of the band’s sound throughout the album, so in that sense, Tsubame isn’t necessarily doing anything radically different from the rest of the record. What makes it stand out to me instead is its execution. Super Climbing Club is, by and large, a remarkably cohesive album, so it isn’t often that one song immediately jumps out from the others. Tsubame, however, manages to do exactly that through a series of memorable moments that keep unfolding from beginning to end. The opening already does a wonderful job of grabbing your attention. It actually reminds me a little of how Utada Hikaru opens One Last Kiss, with Hina briefly breaking away from the melody with a quick vocal hook that almost feels like she’s calling you to your feet, inviting you to come along for a leisurely stroll. There’s also a lovely little vocal run at around the 1:05 mark that immediately brought suis from Yorushika to mind, adding even more to the song’s pop sensibilities. Despite all of that though, Super Climbing Club never strays too far from the mountain path that defines the album. Almost immediately afterward, the band slips into a cheeky Appalachian-inspired passage complete with hoedown-like fiddle, making it feel as though you’ve wandered onto a scenic hiking trail. Then, just when you think they’ve shown all their cards, the song makes a wonderfully seamless transition around the 2:12 mark into a jazzy bossa nova groove. If I had to say, Tsubame was the track that surprised me the most. Prior to this review, I wasn’t overly familiar with Super Climbing Club beyond occasionally seeing their name pop up alongside bands I already followed, so hearing them navigate so many different musical ideas genuinely impressed me. ０７・意志拾い/ishi hiroiAbout halfway up the trail, Super Climbing Club decides to take a well-earned breather with Ishi hiroi. Not that the climb has exactly been strenuous up to this point. Quite the opposite, actually. The first half of Super Climbing Club unfolds at a wonderfully relaxed pace, with each song naturally flowing into the next. Comparatively though, Ishi hiroi feels even more unhurried, stripping back some of the production heard throughout the earlier tracks in favor of something that sounds a little more candid while still retaining the band’s ensemble approach to making music. The image that always comes to mind is that of the band stopping for a few minutes along the trail, taking in the scenery before casually picking up their instruments and playing whatever comes to them in the moment. There’s an effortless quality to the performance that makes it feel weightless and carefree. It’s also here that guitarist Ishikawa Yuu steps forward to share vocal duties with Hina, giving the song a male-female twin vocal arrangement. I thought the layering between their voices was beautifully handled, but more than that, I really enjoyed how naturally they played off one another. Neither voice ever feels like it’s competing for the spotlight; instead, they complement each other in a way that fits the band’s warm, communal sound perfectly. I also appreciated this as a midpoint in the album. Up until now, Super Climbing Club had established a fairly consistent musical identity, so hearing them introduce another vocalist this far into the record was an unexpected but very welcome surprise. If anything, I actually came away wishing they’d explored this dynamic a little more often. There’s an added musicality that comes with having two distinct vocalists to work with, and while I would’ve loved to hear more of it, there’s also something to be said for keeping it in their back pocket and only bringing it out when the moment feels right. １０・樹海/jukai feat. TENDREThe last song I wanted to highlight before moving on to my overall thoughts is Jukai, featuring singer-songwriter and producer Kawahara Taro, better known by his solo moniker TENDRE. I’ll admit, this collaboration completely caught me off guard. Based on what I’d come to know about Super Climbing Club over the course of the album and what I already knew of TENDRE’s music, I never would’ve guessed there’d be much overlap between the two. At the same time though, it also helps put into perspective where Super Climbing Club currently stands within the Japanese music scene. Being able to collaborate with an already established artist like TENDRE speaks to just how much respect they’ve garnered from their peers. Perhaps as a direct consequence of that collaboration, Jukai ends up feeling like one of the album’s biggest departures stylistically. One moment you’re leisurely walking through the woods alongside the band, and the next you’re suddenly transported into what feels like a grand symphonic jazz performance (lol). Mind you, this isn’t the first time we’ve heard Super Climbing Club flirt with jazz. Tsubame already hinted at those influences earlier in the album. It was fascinating, though, hearing them lean so much further into that side of their sound here. More than anything else, Jukai also reaffirmed something I’d been thinking since the opening stretch of the album regarding Hina’s vocals. Her lower register has such a warm, full-bodied quality to it that I honestly think, in another world, she could’ve made for an incredible jazz or R&B vocalist. Hearing her sing against this kind of orchestral accompaniment only made that thought stronger. Speaking of the arrangement itself, I don’t often find myself talking about symphonic music here on the Exchange/Rate, but I genuinely thought the accompaniment was breathtaking. From what I’ve gathered reading discussions surrounding the song online, the version included on Super Climbing Club is actually a shortened one, with live performances extending the instrumental outro quite a bit further. I haven’t had the chance to hear that version for myself yet, but if the recording here is anything to go by, I can absolutely understand why people describe it as such a magical experience. As unexpected as Jukai initially felt within the context of the album, I ultimately came away appreciating it as both a wonderful standalone piece and an exciting glimpse into another avenue Super Climbing Club could continue exploring in future releases. ＜Ｗｈａｔ Ｉ ｔｈｉｎｋ ｏｆ Ｓｕｐｅｒ Ｃｌｉｍｂｉｎｇ Ｃｌｕｂ ＞ Climbing a mountain alone is arguably one of the most ambitious things a person can set out to do. It’s a physically demanding undertaking whose greatest reward often isn’t something tangible, but rather the quiet sense of accomplishment that comes from knowing you reached the summit through your own efforts. Bring other people into that journey though, climbing alongside friends who all share the same goal, and it transforms into something else entirely. It becomes a collective effort; one built on camaraderie, trust, and the shared ambition of reaching the top together. That’s ultimately what I find to be at the heart of Super Climbing Club’s identity. Throughout Super Climbing Club, I got the distinct impression that this is a band driven by a genuine desire to create together. Their chemistry shines through in the way they perform, arrange their music, and constantly build upon one another’s ideas. The album is filled with moments that speak not only to their technical ability, but also to how much they enjoy making music with each other. Ambition, in and of itself, isn’t inherently a good or bad thing. It’s simply what pushes people to pursue greater heights, and when paired with belief in yourself and the people around you, it often leads to wonderful things. Ironically enough, I think that same ambition is both Super Climbing Club‘s greatest strength and its biggest weakness. Earlier, I mentioned that the album itself almost feels like a mountain to climb. At fourteen tracks in total, even accounting for the opening instrumental Departure, it can admittedly look a little intimidating before you’ve even pressed play. Having now reached the end of that journey myself, I do think Super Climbing Club may have been just a touch too ambitious in how much they tried to fit onto a single debut album. Personally, I could’ve seen the record benefiting from a bit more restraint. If the album had, for example, concluded around Ishi hiroi, I think that entire stretch would’ve formed an incredibly cohesive listening experience, perfectly capturing the feeling of setting out on a hike from sunrise to midday. Everything that follows is still enjoyable, but it doesn’t always contribute to that same vivid sense of place the first half establishes so beautifully. At the same time though, it’s difficult for me to criticize the band too harshly for that decision because I also understand exactly where it came from. This feels like the work of a group of musicians who simply had so many ideas they were excited to share that they couldn’t bear to leave any of them behind. Even when I found myself wishing the album had been a little more concise, I never stopped admiring just how polished the musicianship remained throughout. And perhaps that’s the greatest accomplishment of Super Climbing Club. Much like climbing an actual mountain, reaching the end of the journey is rewarding in and of itself. By the time I arrived at the summit, I couldn’t help but look back at everything Super Climbing Club had accomplished across the album with a real sense of admiration. All in all, I think Super Climbing Club is a wonderful debut, and one that leaves me genuinely excited to see just how much higher Super Climbing Club can climb from here. ＜Ｍｙ Ｒａｔｉｎｇ＞４.５ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ ５ ＆ ９ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ １０ An album having “too many songs” is, in most cases, hardly a problem to me. If anything, I’m usually happy to have more music to listen to, barring the occasional release that simply rounds out its tracklist with previously released singles and calls it a day. Thankfully, Super Climbing Club never really falls into that trap. Instead, it comes across as an album made by a band eager to show just how much they have to offer. Could it have benefited from being a little more concise? I certainly think so. At the same time though, it’s also far from being an exhausting listen. Quite the opposite, actually. There’s such a refreshing quality to Super Climbing Club’s music that even across fourteen tracks, I rarely found myself wanting to stop listening. If anything, I simply came away wishing the journey had been a little more focused rather than any shorter. ーー What are your guys’ thoughts on Super Climbing Club’s self-titled debut album, Super Climbing Club? Let us know down in the comments! Likewise, we’d love to hear if there are any albums that have made you want to pick up and learn an instrument. Whether it was the guitar, piano, drums, trumpet, or something else entirely, be sure to share them with us! Before I let you guys go, don’t forget to check out Al’s review of yubiori2 over at the Omunibasu Substack if you haven’t yet already. As always, it’s fun seeing how we each approached this month’s theme from completely different angles. Happy Listening!

items.body:
Paris's Latency imprint surveys the harp's enduring charm on 'Eleven Harps', commissioning eleven exclusive solo compositions from some of the world's most vital players, including Ahya Simone, Sissi Rada, Mary Lattimore, Nailah Hunter and Miriam Adefris.

One of the civilization's musical staples, the harp has been in constant use for thousands of years, developed seemingly independently in ancient China, Western Asia and Africa and sticking around despite its cumbersome size. Of course, they don't have to be huge, but part of the appeal is the resonance of strings that are often as tall as a person. At the minute it's a niche speciality but one that's still at least visible; commonly used in classical music and folk, it's also become a fixture in jazz and R&B thanks to artists like Alice Coltrane and Dorothy Ashby's crucial early work. And now it's even fairly common to come across harp in experimental circles, a recent reality that Latency are keen to examine on 'Eleven Harps'.

Tapping some of the international scene's most intriguing players, figures who work in ambient, jazz, contemporary music and the high avant garde, the label have assembled a vivid picture of the instrument as it stands in 2026, highlighting the range of approaches. Kicking off the set is London-based Austrian-Ethiopian artist Miriam Adefris, who's best known for her work with Floating Points and Shabaka Hutchings. She appeared on Latency last year with 'Plunge', her debut album with her trio Flur and her contribution 'Amber' is another sublime manifestation of her skill as a player, a producer and an arranger. The harp is at the center of the sound, but Adefris is able to extend its range with subtle electronic elements and electroacoustic textures. It's an approach that Mary Lattimore's very familiar with at this stage and her lullaby-like 'We Take Turns Crying' matches her chiming phrases with fittingly Badalamenti-inspired synth strings.

Perhaps predictably, the highlight of the collection comes from Sissi Rada, who follows February's outstanding 'Nana Butu' with the theatrical 'Archilochus' Fragments', a track that seems to bend time itself. Paying respect to iambic poet Archilochus, Makropoulou plays the role of bard and Greek chorus teasing out bewitching melodies from her instrument and accompanying them with terrifying wails, Pythagorean dissonances and disorienting sub bass. Elsewhere, Swiss artist Loréleï Nelle travels further into the unknown with 'S/Tern Tone', matching clattering extended technique toolbox with suitably haunted synthwork. Detroit's Ahya Simone, who's worked with Kelela, Sudan Archives and Shigeto, among others, closes the set with the meditative echoes of 'Kooky Fish'.

items.body:
Arca's new studio album "XXXXX" arriving via XL Recordings.

"Five years after the twice GRAMMY-nominated KiCk i and subsequent KICK pentalogy, the Venezuelan-born musician, producer, vocalist, and visual artist returns with her first full-length album since concluding one of the most ambitious chapters in contemporary music.

If the KICK era expanded Arca's universe outward, XXXXX turns inward and fractures it apart. Across 16 tracks, the album excavates vastly different emotional landscapes to deliver a body of work that is darker, more aggressive, more experimental, and unwilling to settle into fixed form. Initially conceived as a mixtape before revealing itself as an album, XXXXX embraces contradiction as a core methodology. In the spirit of her previous mixtapes @@@@@ (2020)—released as a 62-minute single—and &&&&& (2013), XXXXX thrives on raw exploration and instinct. It arrives as a deliberate interruption of expectation.

“It seems playful, also mischievous, to interrupt that autopilot,” says Arca.

The album's striking artwork depicts Arca as a biomechanical entity, accompanied by two owls—symbols of protection and the underworld in Greek mythology. Like the music itself, the imagery inhabits a space between worlds where transformation is both terrifying and liberatory. Suspended between posthuman augmentation and raw emotion, XXXXX exposes the mainframe. It is a record born from uncertainty, contradiction, instinct, and surrender—a becoming-machine that continues Arca's lifelong project of redefining what it means to be human both in, and against, the machine.

For Arca, rebirth has never been a metaphor, but a practice. She continues to exist in multiple states simultaneously, collapsing boundaries between human and machine, high and low culture, and experimental noise and pop music. Following her first-ever painting exhibition at London’s ICA earlier this year, XXXXX arrives as the latest transmission from a continuously evolving creative process. Over the last year, Arca has remained prolific: unveiling the double-sided single "Puta" / "Sola"; remixing tracks for Addison Rae, Robyn, and Hikaru Utada; collaborating with Tokischa on “Chama”; and contributing production to Madonna’s CONFESSIONS II. She walked the runways and made appearances at major international fashion weeks, while also composing the original motion picture soundtrack for Stillz’s film, Barrio Triste.

Now, after years of transformation beneath the surface, her next musical evolution reveals itself."

Trust Rabit’s Halcyon Veil to highlight São Paolo’s grimy anomaly Agazero, and his distorted skews of drill, jungle, and funk bruxaria convention.

Agazero is just one strand of pursuit by Eric Alves, who also spends his energies on work as ICQbaby, DJ LHC, 177th, Arizona4K, Partículas Occults, and Vóid. On’ Dissidente’ he flashes rude fang in six parts spanning bloodied drill with Arabic strings in ‘Of Sonic Agnosia’, thru crunching darkside baile rhythm and squealing electronics ft. KARAN! & Yandrel in ‘amidst Backstage Hostility’, to reveal a taste for piquant, bittersweet hooks in ‘Europeanized Atrophy’, and rounding out with a mean flourish of squashed D&B breaks, psy-techno roil and nu metal snarl like Craxxxsmurf x Croww with ‘Into Hermetic Isolation (The End of it All)’.

Viscerally fresh gear for the freaks.

items.body:
Berlin/Bristol’s bass don piles on and refines the ‘nuum pressure in acres of noirish jazz space for Italy’s XCPT, generating some of his starkest and strongest material, advised to fans of Wax Doctor, Healing Force Project, Photek, Demdike Stare...

With the ‘Airdrop’ trilogy of fractious, ‘unum-surfing collages tucked away from Peak Oil, Low End Activist indulges formative passions for jazz-inflected late ’90s D&B and Y2K tension on ‘JH Versions’. He effectively joins the dots of his brittle, pointillist drum programming with spectral vestiges of ‘70s jazz fusion and neo-noir film music in a similar way to Photek or Wax Doctor, but with more grime (and dark garage) under the cuticles, nailing an ideal of rugged late night music that deftly swerves cliche, or at least tweaks the tropes to his own ends.

‘Midnight’ strikes with a martial percussive discipline veiled by goth jazz keys and whispers, beside the stoned/drunken-master warehouse swerve and haunted dancehall of ‘Sapphire’ going like Photek meets The Caretaker. The depth-charged subs and ricochet drums of ‘Ultramarine’ feel like shadowboxing underwater to a crowd of sirens, and ‘Celeste’ plumbs the deepest levels of dark garage skip and blunted jazz, somewhere between Healing Force Project and Burial, while ‘Indigo’ signs off with creaking echoes of Wax Doctor’s louche, syncopated flex and Pat Thomas’ jazz jungle throwback.

items.body:
Doom metal staples The Body are depicted at early crests of their powers on an expanded reissue of their 2013 EP, bolstered with debut single ‘Cop Killer / Dead Cops’ (2005) and unreleased bonus, all remastered for extra pressure.

Few bands shiver the timbers quite like The Body, whose loud, crashing drums, shrieks and detuned axes alloy the fiercest doom metal forms on ‘Master, We Perish’. The original EP’s siren-sounding cataclysm ‘The Ebb and Flow of Tides in a Sea of Ash’ fronts a session taking in the quiet/loud tension of choral wafts calving into heck on ‘The Blessed Lay Down and Writhe in Agony’, and the 9 mins of trampling industrial doom to ‘Worship’, all recorded during the phase that prompted their debut Thrill Jockey LP ‘Christs, Redeemers’.

The EP now extends to include earliest flashpoint that first pinned them on the map, with the hackled drama of ‘Cop Killer’ and ‘Dead Cop’ emblematic of the mid ‘00s Providence, Rhode Island scene that birthed them, while the parting ‘untitled’ piece clambers out of a drone hole to give it full frontal for the freaks.

items.body:
Sunn O))) guest players and Ideologic Organ mainstays Jessika Kenney and Eyvind Kang return with six new pieces for voice, viola, setar and electronics.

Recorded in Istanbul, Seattle and Bologna, The Face Of The Earth is more obviously Eastern in tone to the duo's last IO offering, Aestuarium. Taking its cue from classical Persian and Javanese traditions, and themed around the idea of "drawing the binary from the unary, like reflections from a mirror, and its inverse, the concealed identity", it's a collection of sonic riddles whose meaning can be unlocked, at least to some extent, by the "reading cards" provided in the insert. Despite the arcane mysticism at work, it's music of self-evident and ravishing beauty: from the medievalist balladry of 'Tavaf', to the pensive but restlessly percussive 'Kidung', Kenney's vocal performances are show-stopping throughout, and Kang's strings resonate powerfully around them. Over its short duration, the sparse voice and viola interplay of 'Ordered Pairs II' take on the character of spiritual jazz, while the looping and phasing techniques applied on 'Mirror Stage' come over like a courtly response to Steve Reich's 'It's Gonna Rain', and 'The Face Of The Earth' feels like the logical extension of the more avant-garde moments on Julia Holter's Ekstasis. Tremendous stuff.

items.body:
Psych duo Bear Bones, Lay Low naturally adapt to soundtrack dimensions with a richly atmospheric, electroacoustic accompaniment to Léonard Pongo’s titular film, benefitting from Laszlo Umbreit’s experience in this arena.

“Discrepant presents the LP edition of Tales from the Source, the original film soundtrack by Bear Bones, Lay Low and Laszlo Umbreit. Originally composed for Belgian-Congolese artist Léonard Pongo’s 2024 film of the same name, this release reworks the film's audio into a continuous, fluid listening experience.

The album is built on a direct contrast between heavy electronic manipulation and raw environmental audio. Laszlo Umbreit captured the foundation of the record through field recordings and additional electronics, focusing on the quiet, tactile sounds of water, riverbeds, and natural spaces. These recordings were then processed and expanded by Bear Bones, Lay Low, who layered the tracks using synthesizers, samplers and various effects processors.

Rather than acting as a standard background score, the music functions as a detailed piece of environmental sound art. The tracks are edited to blend into one another without distinct gaps, mirroring the slow pace and visual flow of the film. Through the use of tape loops, filtering, and electronic processing, the natural landscapes are systematically distorted and rearranged. The result is a dark, slow-moving suite of electroacoustic music that strips away traditional melody to focus entirely on texture, resonance, and the changing dynamics of the recorded environments.”

items.body:
2nd wave dub techno staple Stephen Hitchell meets new wave producer Federson in a back ’n forth of timeless originals and versions.

San Francisco’s Chris Kelly, aka Federsen’s Alt Dub label hosts this passing of the baton/torch with CV313 and Echospace figure Hitchell a sits 2nd release after the ‘Positive Charge’ EP  christened the vessel in earlier ’24. Federsen fronts the session with a smoky, night-driving dub of CV313’s ‘Skycrossing’ in properly classic Maurizio style, especially that scooping bassline, whilst shutting it down with the more air-stepping levity of his dusted congas and distant dub chords to ‘Skyway’.

CV313’s original ‘Skycrossing’ places his mastery of constantly shifting, ever the same, dynamic within its unfurling envelopes, alongside a remix of ‘Skyway’ that plunges upward, outward into billowing electro-acoustic dub techno dimensions.

items.body:
Tobias Freund’s roots in ‘80s & ‘90s pop engineering - for Milli Vanilli, Meat Loaf, Scatman John! - are touched-up in a 2nd parade of cover versions, of The Human League, This Heat, Japan, Suicide, Heaven 17, and Harold Budd & Brian Eno

Perhaps best known to many for his run of classic ’00s minimal techno as Tobias., the German producer’s binds run much deeper than that sound, with engineering credits on the likes of Lassigue Bendthaus’ pivotal EBM album ‘Matter’, as well as those that paid the bills (Milli Vanilli, Meat Loaf). ‘Plenty Of Time With Nothing To Do’ now catches him returning to formative passions with ample technical knowledge earned over the decades, generating a mix of faithful and daring takes on evergreens and personal faves augmented with inventive, playful nuance.

Tobias.’ freunds are vocal foils, with Barbie Williams perfectly emulating Andrea Conway’s dreamy delivery of Dome’s ‘Cruel When Complete’, subtly reset in dusty triplets, while Romina Schopf drily glazes the tribal groove of their take on This Heat’s ‘Twilight Furniture’, and Argenis Brito channels David Sylvian with a Latin accent in the re-do of Japan’s ‘My New Career’. The ‘floor is also attended on Gudrun Gut’s standout, breathy revision of Suicide’s ‘Girl’, and Tobias. himself even makes an appearance, pitched alien-like on a puckered revision of The Human League’s ‘Morale’, another highpoint along with Uwe Schmidt aka Atom™ reprising his LB ‘Pop Artificielle’ steez on a remake of Heaven 17’s ‘The Best Kept Secret’.

The first smoke signals of Photek’s keenly awaited ‘Form & Function 3’ emerge in this taut roller delivered on his new label, reMod

items.body:
Smiling C embrace the C.21st with a volley of trance-to-downbeat electronics by Ilian Tape alum Jahandar Hamidieh aka Fields of Mist, tipped FFO Aleksi Perälä, Avenir, the Analord.

‘planetary mist signatures’ hails a marked departure from Smiling C’s broad ’70s-‘90s touchstones, including a recent run of AOR and soft rock, in pursuit of a shimmering, modernist electronic spirit. Sifted from “lost B sides, long tracks, random jams…” the 14 parts add up to a mazy mosaic portrait of FoM’s livewire take on structures, genres, which emerged in the mid-later ‘90s and still hold sway over producers today. 

They surely resemble morsels registered in the artist’s handful of drops for Munich’s Ilian Tape, but given more room to spread out and play to the full spectrum of his thing, encompassing the iridescent trance-techno of ‘from another system’ thru the puckered electro pearl ‘ES-1 H3500’, via superb piece of ambient electro in ‘bio-komputer waveforms’ recalling Bitstream’s custom-built pulses, to breezier electro-house on ‘routine drive maintenance’, and the urban Tribe-esque Detroit beatdown of ‘in halfweg’.

items.body:
Skewed dub specialist label Blundar host a mutant cumbia dub haunting by Bogotá’s ezmeralda, a leading figure of wayward ambient shook up from the Latin American bush of ghosts...

Preceded by an LP for Tra Tra Trax’s Ambie-Tón divison, and an EP with Éter Editions, ezmeralda continues to stake out a unique sort of tresillo metaphysics perhaps familiar to fans of Debit’s Modern Love albums or Elijah Minnelli fancies, or even The Caretaker’s slant on dusty ballroom standards, but applied to traditional cumbia. Everything inside is slowed and diffused to a vaporous crawl; bone-rubbed rhythms and basslines smudged into oblivion, and air hashed with spectral traces of flutes and accordions; ancient cries heard thru a modern lens.

For 16 minutes ezmeralda suspends perceptions of time and space with a sublime, deferred gratification, never quite fully revealing the forms, operating by suggestion in finely extracted and layered arrangements. The A-side feels as though we’re shored-up on some Mangrove-covered Caribbean coastline of Colombia at night, threats lurking below the briny surface and thick in the air, before the B-side brings the phantoms forward in what feels like Pole processing Elijah Minnelli’s anachronistic cumbia blooz...

items.excerpt: Death Is Not The End unearth Ercilia Costa’s haunting 1920’s and 1930’s Portuguese Fado recordings made in Madrid As played in the label’s 20’s & 30’s Fado Special for NTS, Ercilia’s songs epitomise the melancholy elegance of Fado, a style of Portuguese folk music with roots in Moorish guitar music, and connections to old Portuguese trading routes and colonies. more
items.body:
Death Is Not The End unearth Ercilia Costa’s haunting 1920’s and 1930’s Portuguese Fado recordings made in Madrid

As played in the label’s 20’s & 30’s Fado Special for NTS, Ercilia’s songs epitomise the melancholy elegance of Fado, a style of Portuguese folk music with roots in Moorish guitar music, and connections to old Portuguese trading routes and colonies.

items.body: German multi-instrumentalist Udo Schindler has been recording and releasing music relentlessly over the last few years. The reviews below offer a glimpse of just some of his production over the first half of this year. Udo Schindler and Elisabeth Harnik – Poetry of Friction (arch-musik, 2026) To his immense credit, architect of buildings (by day) and sounds (by night) Udo Schindler is tireless and itinerant. He has some of core collaborators – see Harald Kimmig and Eric Zwang Eriksson on Imprints of Experiences below – but, more often, he pushes his music forward by performing with new musicians. Presumably, this forces him and his collaborators to adapt to each other on the spot, and in the process explore unanticipated sonic territories. Poetry of Friction captures Schindler on tenor sax, clarinet, and cornet in a duo with Elisabeth Harnik on Bechstein piano (in and out) at a May 2025 performance at Musik- & Pianohaus Schwinghammer in Weilheim in Oberbayern, Germany. The affair is largely muted. Both Harnik and Schindler have been studying extended techniques and uncustomary articulations for years, and as should be of no surprise given the title, they continue to do so here, focusing on frictions, burbles, and heavy vibrations rather than anything crisp or ostensibly melodic. If one were to consider this a duel, Schindler has found his match in Harnik, who just as adeptly swings from idiomatic to non-idiomatic techniques. Some passages are blustery and beautiful. Some are hardly audible, roughly textured flutters and other understated soundscaping. Whichever way the duo veers, however, Schindler and Harnik stay linked and measured, wandering wide spaces but most often in tandem, which finds an unexpected potential in the soulful and dramatic climax and release of its final minutes. Poetry of Friction is available as a download on Bandcamp. Poetry of Friction by Udo Schindler & Elisabeth Harnik Udo Schindler and Sergio Armaroli – Transalpine Sound Bridges (Munich-Milan) (Fundacja Słuchaj, 2026) Transalpine Sound Bridges is the oddball of the group. Whereas the other releases were recorded live in studio or in front of an audience, this album came out of a canceled duo gig. As no in person collaboration had (or has yet) taken place, Sergio Armaroli responded by recording a series of vibraphone and percussion solos for Schindler (soprano sax, clarinets, flute, cornet) to improvise over. The result is a music that wafts through space. As the other releases here attest, Schindler can honk, contort, and scream with the best of them. Here, likely inspired by Armaroli’s dreamy runs on the vibraphone, Schindler also shows that he can lean into minimalist, calmer motifs. One hears his expert control, but in restraint rather than this John Butcher-like acrobatics. This album reflects on some remote Alpine mountain range rather than conquering the Großglockner’s peak. In a sense, this is impressionist more than expressionist, which is notable given the improvisations have taken place remotely. It grapples with that tension in the colorful patchworks of yielding and unyielding pastures, unsteady breezes, a panorama of beautiful flowers juxtaposed to barren crags, peace with a soft undertone or playful danger. Consider Transalpine Sound Bridges yet another side of Schindler that ranges from the bucolic and airy to the positively bluesy, coaxed in those directions by Armaroli’s knottily vining solo chasses and the vagaries of circumstance. Available as a double CD and download from bandcamp. Transalpine Sound Bridges [Munich-Milano] 2CD by Udo Schindler & Sergio Armaroli Udo Schindler and Uwe Oberg – Schädel-Magie (FMR, 2026) The title, Schädel-Magie , is German for skull magic, which sounds quite macabre. But maybe we should think of it in terms of sounds bouncing around the inner caverns of the head, in the eardrums and the auditory cortex and amygdala, rather than something more sinister. The skull in this analogy is self-evident, and the magic lay in the music produced, received, and processed. (A quick internet search tells me sound processing is an extremely complicated and weird, and in that sense quasi-magical, process, as much higher brain functioning is.) The album, Schädel-Magie, features Schindler on various clarinets and alto flute, and Uwe Oberg on piano (like Harnik, in and out) and captures the duo in studio in 2024. The track titles are untranslatable (or nonsensical?) compound nouns invented by the late German poet Thomas Kling. If the words themselves do not quite carry over into English (what the hell is a body-branch or night machine?) the collectivity of the sounds are universal and perform a universal linguo-emotive magic of their own. Schädel-Magie begins as a wild and winding romp but quickly dissipates into extended passages of piano and saxophone constructivism. From there, Schindler and Oberg shift into a series of noirish pieces that explore a range of techniques and dynamics, though always drawn to some dark, mysterious corner. Or a winding staircase at the darkest part of night, wherein nothing nefarious has to happen but various anxious potentialities nevertheless reside in its shadows. As much as anything else, Schädel-Magie distinguishes itself from the other albums reviewed here in its mood – even in its tender moments one senses something cryptic, if not also haunting – and its barbed-wire spiraling. Schädel-Magie is available via the arc-musik website: https://arch-musik.de/project/schaedel-magie/ . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
Before getting into the controversy, Massive Attack’s Singapore concert on 29 July was, in this writer’s opinion, far and away the best show the country has seen this year. It was transcendent, thought-provoking and deeply moving — the kind of performance that reminded you what live music can achieve when sound, visuals, politics, and emotion come together with absolute purpose.

The British trip-hop pioneers did not simply play a collection of songs. They built an overwhelming audiovisual experience that felt urgent, unsettling, and profoundly human. And yet, one of the biggest conversations to emerge from the night has not been about the concert itself. Instead, it has been about a flag.

Near the end of the performance at The Star Theatre, Massive Attack members Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall held up a Palestinian flag as the audience cheered. Del Naja then said “Free Palestine”, after which members of the crowd independently took up the chant.

In the days after the show, Singapore Police confirmed that reports had been lodged and investigations were ongoing. The Infocomm Media Development Authority also said it was investigating a possible breach of the concert’s licence conditions.

Concert promoter Lushington Entertainments said it was aware of the reports and would “fully cooperate with the relevant authorities as required”.

The band also told the audience that it had removed a song from its setlist because of “local laws”, although it did not elaborate further. At the time of writing, the authorities have not confirmed which song was omitted or why.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Adele Chan 🇸🇬 (@adele__chan)

For readers unfamiliar with the controversy, Singapore does not allow the public display of foreign national emblems without a permit or exemption. Those convicted of doing so may face a fine of up to S$500, imprisonment of up to six months, or both.

That explains why the authorities have the power to investigate the incident. It does not make the situation any less ridiculous. There was no reported violence. No threat to the audience. No indication that the concert became unsafe. Two musicians held up a flag, members of the crowd cheered, and the show came to an end.

Yet somewhere between the stage lights going down and everyone heading home, the moment became a police and regulatory matter. Massive Attack raised a Palestinian flag. Singapore raised an investigation. Only here could an expression of solidarity generate this much paperwork.

To be clear, visiting artists are not exempt from local laws. Musicians, promoters, and venues are expected to comply with the conditions attached to their performances, whether or not they personally agree with them. But legality and proportionality are not the same thing. A regulation may provide grounds for an investigation without making that investigation sensible, necessary, or remotely proportionate to what actually happened. Context should matter.

Massive Attack were not encouraging violence. They were not promoting an armed organisation. They were not placing the audience in danger or transforming the venue into an unsafe environment. They displayed a flag associated with the Palestinian people and voiced their support for Palestinian freedom. A Palestinian flag is not the flag of Hamas. Support for Palestinian civilians, dignity, freedom, or statehood should not automatically be treated as a threat to public order.

Yet the official response risks blurring that distinction. It turns a brief gesture of solidarity into something suspicious enough to warrant police reports, licensing scrutiny, and the possibility of criminal penalties. And for what?

The audience saw the flag. Some concertgoers cheered. Others may have disagreed. The country did not descend into chaos. The performance ended. Singapore remained standing. The political nature of the gesture should not have surprised anyone either.

Massive Attack have spent decades incorporating questions of war, state power, surveillance, inequality, and human rights into their work. Their politics are not an inconvenient addition to their music. They are woven into the group’s identity and creative output.

In 2025, the band also helped establish a collective supporting musicians who had spoken out about Israel’s military actions in Gaza, alleging that artists faced intimidation and pressure within the music industry for doing so. Political expression is not an unexpected interruption at a Massive Attack concert. It is part of the concert.

Fans do not attend their shows expecting the uncomfortable parts of the world to be neatly edited out. They go knowing the group has something to say and that the performance may ask more of them than passive enjoyment. That does not mean every audience member must agree with the band. It means artists should be able to articulate a position without every uncomfortable gesture being escalated into a potential public-order issue.

Singaporeans often joke that complaining is a national pastime. Something happens. Someone takes offence. A report gets filed. Suddenly, a moment that might otherwise have passed becomes an official matter requiring statements, investigations, and administrative attention.

That instinct can be useful when genuine harm has occurred. But not every source of discomfort is dangerous. Not every disagreement demands intervention. And not everything that happens on a concert stage needs to become a police report. The urge to complain about anything remotely contentious can produce a society that is orderly but increasingly unable to distinguish between actual harm and simple unease. A flag may make some people uncomfortable. Discomfort is not disorder.

There is also a wider concern for Singapore’s live music scene. The country has worked hard to establish itself as a major touring destination in Asia. International artists, promoters, and fans increasingly view Singapore as a reliable stop for arena concerts, theatre performances, and large-scale cultural events.

But a thriving concert ecosystem cannot be built solely on efficient venues, clean facilities, and orderly crowds. It also requires space for artists to be artists. Music has never existed outside politics. From protest songs and benefit concerts to stage speeches and visual statements, musicians have always used live performance to respond to the world around them.

Audiences are capable of encountering those ideas. They can applaud, disagree, remain silent, walk away, or argue about them after the lights come on. That exchange is part of what gives live music its meaning. It is not disorder. It is culture.

That was especially evident during Massive Attack’s performance. The show was moving precisely because it refused to separate art from the world that produced it. Its visuals, music, and messages worked together to confront the audience with questions of violence, power, and human suffering. Removing that political dimension would not have made the concert more neutral. It would have made it less honest.

The authorities will determine whether Massive Attack breached the conditions attached to their performance licence. But the public is equally entitled to ask whether an alleged breach deserved this degree of scrutiny in the first place. A Palestinian flag appeared at a concert. It did not place the audience in danger. It did not threaten Singapore’s stability. It did not require a national demonstration of bureaucratic efficiency.

Perhaps, instead of rushing to complain, report, and investigate, we could acknowledge the moment for what it was: a political gesture by an openly political band during one of the most remarkable concerts Singapore has hosted this year. Massive Attack raised a flag. The crowd responded. The music continued. Perhaps we should have simply allowed the moment to speak for itself.

items.body:
I7HVN Returns To Qilla Records With 'On The Hill', Leaning Into Raw & Hypnotic Techno

31 July 2026

Previously Bangalore-based and now Indore-based artist Ishan Gaur aka I7HVN just marked his return to Qilla Records with the EP 'On The Hill', coming back to the seminal Indian techno label after 2023's 'Youthful'. The 8-track release featuring 5 originals and 3 remixes by Caldera, Kabeer Arora and Spain's 矯激 [Radical] is Gaur's 3rd EP this year, following 'Priests of Decay' and the launch of his alternative moniker, ruag, with 'jester'.

While 'Priests Of Decay' featured a more abstract and cerebral take on techno, 'On The Hill' makes things more tangible as it adheres to the dark and hypnotic strains associated with the label, counting on the genre's repetitive nature to make things feel ceremonial and visceral. Unlike 'Priests Of Decay', every element asserts its own identity to draw and guide your attention, specially on more straightforward raw techno tracks like 'Vulture' or the minimal-almost-ambient 'On The Hill'.

I7HVN's experimental instinct comes through on the atonal sounds of 'Kangling' that feel almost kinesthetic in nature, while 'Luminarism' decorates its breakdown with personal voice notes and sentimental piano tinkering to include emotional drama in the otherwise low-end-led EP.

Listen to 'On The Hill' below and follow I7HVN for more information.
